units.title: Plasticity in practice: skills, training, development and ageing

lessons.title: What a skill is, neurally: components, stages and why 'the skill area' is a category error
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to define a skill operationally, list the components any skill claim has to specify, and explain why the question 'which part of the brain stores this skill?' usually cannot be answered as asked. A skill is a reliably reproducible change in what a person can do, measured on a task, that survives a delay and is not explained by a single lucky attempt. The phrase 'a skill is stored in area X' bundles at least five separable things: the sensory information the performer extracts, the internal model that predicts what the body and the world will do next, the motor command selected, the error signal used to correct it, and the task environment that supplies the feedback in the first place. A claim about a skill is only as precise as its treatment of these components. The electronic textbook Neuroscience Online makes the components concrete. In Section 3, Chapter 3, sub-section 3.5, 'Encoding of Movement by Motor Cortex', the textbook describes how single cells in primary motor cortex change firing with the direction of a movement (see the directional tuning figure 3.8), and sub-section 3.10, 'Premotor cortex neurons signal preparation for movement', describes cells whose activity tracks an upcoming movement before it happens. In Chapter 4, sub-section 4.6, 'Functions of the Basal Ganglia', the same textbook introduces the cortico-basal ganglia loop, and sub-sections 4.8 and 4.9 turn to 'Habit learning in striatum' and to patients with basal ganglia disorders who are impaired at learning tasks while being able to perform already-learned movements. Chapter 5 then assigns the cerebellum a role in error correction and prediction. Read together, these sections already imply that 'the' skill is not in one place: preparation, selection, correction and execution are handled by different circuits, and a good example of this division is the way a well-practised movement starts to run with less moment-to-moment sensory guidance. Three qualifications keep the claim honest. First, firing that correlates with a movement direction does not show that the cells cause the movement, nor that they 'store' it; population decoding of a variable is evidence that the variable is represented, not that the representation is the memory itself. Second, skill learning is not one process. Adaptation experiments, sequence-learning experiments and real-world expertise tasks measure different things and produce different dissociations, which is why the review 'Multiple systems for motor skill learning' argues that several learning systems contribute with different time courses rather than one system serving 'skill'. Third, stage language ('cognitive', 'associative', 'autonomous') is a description of performance changes over practice, not a claim about a switch being thrown in a particular structure. Used as a description, it is useful; used as a mechanism, it overreaches.
lessons.example: Work the components through a laboratory task, then check one popular number. In a force-field reaching experiment, a participant makes point-to-point reaches while a robotic handle pushes the hand sideways. Performance is measured as the deviation from the straight line to the target. Early in training the hand is pushed off course and the participant corrects visibly; after a few hundred trials the path is straight again, which means the motor command has been altered to pre-empt the push. The decisive measurement is not the straight path but the after-effect: when the field is switched off, the hand now curves in the opposite direction. That after-effect is the strongest evidence that an internal model changed, because a merely strategic correction (moving deliberately the other way) would not produce the reversed error once the perturbation is gone. Now the arithmetic of the famous shortcut. The popular claim that ten thousand hours of practice produces expertise is a claim about accumulated practice time. Convert it: practising three hours a day, six days a week, is eighteen hours a week. Ten thousand divided by eighteen is 555.6 weeks, and 555.6 divided by 52 is 10.7 years. At four hours a day, seven days a week (twenty-eight hours a week), the same arithmetic gives 357 weeks, or 6.9 years. The arithmetic is fine; the inference it is often used to support is not. Accumulated practice in those studies is estimated retrospectively by asking experts to recall how they trained, the variance in attained performance that practice accounts for depends heavily on the domain and on how performance was measured, and the claim is contested in the literature. In our reaching example the comparable number is not hours at all but trials and error size, and the after-effect measures something practice hours cannot express. Two lessons follow. Use a measurable performance change with a control for strategy, and match the quantity you measure to the quantity the claim is about.
lessons.question: A study reports that expert typists have different motor cortex activity from novices and concludes that motor cortex is where typing skill is stored. Using the component list from this lesson, what is the central problem with the conclusion?
lessons.answer: The study shows a between-group difference in activity during typing; it does not identify the changed component, the cause of the difference, or show that the cell activity is the durable change in performance that the word 'stored' implies.
lessons.distractor: The main problem is that the sample of experts was probably too small to detect a real difference in motor cortex activity.
lessons.correction: Sample size is a secondary worry. The primary problem is a category mistake about what was measured. Activity during a task is a state measure and can reflect the mechanics of the movement, effort or attention, whereas a stored skill claim is about a durable, task-specific change in what the person can do. The sentence also leaps from a necessary involvement of a region to its being the storage site, and it does not separate the components of the task - perception of the text, selection of key sequences, timing, and error correction - which in the textbook evidence sit in different circuits. A defensible claim would name the component that changed, show the change tracks performance rather than effort, and show it requires that circuit.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: a motor command is the set of signals sent to muscles; an internal model is a learned mapping that predicts the sensory consequence of a command (a forward model) or the command needed for a goal (an inverse model); adaptation is a change produced by a perturbation within a session; consolidation here means change that continues or stabilises after practice stops; an after-effect is the error that appears when a perturbation is removed, and it is interpreted as evidence of a changed internal model; retention is performance after a delay; transfer is performance on a task you did not practise; chunking is the grouping of separate actions into one unit executed as a whole. Keep habit distinct: a habit is a learned cue-triggered response that is comparatively insensitive to the value of its outcome, and lesson 68 treats it separately. Expertise is not a synonym for skill in this course: expertise is a high level of attained performance on a defined task.
depth.mechanism: Why would repeated practice produce a durable change rather than a temporary adjustment? Each practice trial generates prediction error: the difference between the sensory feedback the performer expects and what arrives. Error drives an update of the internal model, and the update is expressed as a changed command on subsequent trials; that is why the after-effect appears when the perturbation vanishes. The textbook's cortico-basal ganglia and cerebellar sections supply the division of labour: basal ganglia loops support the selection and reinforcement of actions, the cerebellum supports prediction and the correction of the timing and size of movements, and cortical motor areas hold the mapping from intention to command. The time-course claim in the review 'Multiple systems for motor skill learning' is that these contributions are not synchronous - early performance is dominated by effortful, feedback-dependent control, and later performance is comparatively automatic - and that consolidation processes continuing after the session interact with new learning. The limitations matter as much as the mechanism. First, dissociations between systems in animal work rely on lesions and pharmacological manipulations that are hard to mirror exactly in humans, so the human evidence is largely inference from behaviour and imaging. Second, an observed group difference in activity cannot be ordered in time or assigned a direction of causality by the measure alone. Third, plasticity is not automatically beneficial: a strengthened pathway can encode an error as readily as a solution, and the same mechanisms support unwanted motor habits, which is why the word plasticity should not be read as improvement.
depth.secondExample: Contrast motor learning with a perceptual skill, because the two do not share a mechanism and the same vocabulary hides that. Consider learning to identify bird species by song, or a radiologist learning to spot a subtle fracture. The trainee is not learning a movement sequence; the trainee is learning which features are diagnostic. The evidence you can collect therefore differs: instead of after-effects you measure sensitivity and bias in a discrimination task, search time, and eye-movement patterns that show which regions of a stimulus are inspected. In the perceptual case, improvement can occur with no change in the motor response - the same button press - yet performance can rise dramatically, which no motor-adaptation account predicts. This contrast has a practical consequence for evaluating claims. If a course advertisement promises to 'train your brain' and the trained task is a perceptual discrimination, then evidence about motor adaptation from a completely different task cannot support it. The components must match. A skill claim specifies what the performer detects, decides, and does, and only then can you ask which measurement isolates the change.
depth.mistake: The most common error is 'muscle memory': the belief that a skill is stored in the muscles, or, in its more sophisticated form, that a skill is stored in one cortical patch once practice finishes. The diagnostic marker is a claim of the form 'the skill moved to area X when it became automatic'. The correction is to restate the claim in terms of components and measurements: what changed in the internal model, in the command, or in the sensitivity to diagnostic information, and how was that change measured? A second common error is reading more activity as more learning. Activity is a state measure that rises with effort and novelty, so an expert often shows less task-related activity than a novice in the same region while performing better. A third error is treating a stage label as a mechanism; 'autonomous stage' describes reduced attentional demand, not a physical transfer of a file into a different drawer.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, no submission required. Choose a skill you can practise for twenty minutes: a three-ball cascade toss, typing a short sequence without looking, a repeated chord change, or a mirror-drawing task. Write four lines before you start: (1) the observable performance measure and its units; (2) the perturbation or difficulty that makes error visible; (3) the control condition you would use to rule out a strategy change; (4) the comparison that would test retention (the same measure after a delay, without further practice). Then practise and record the measure at three points: start, after ten minutes, and after a two-minute break. Model response: a strong answer states something like 'measure = mean absolute deviation from the target line in millimetres averaged over ten trials; perturbation = half the trials with an imposed lateral offset; strategy control = compare the size of the reversed error after offset removal with the size predicted by deliberate correction; retention = same measure tomorrow, first ten trials'. Self-review rubric: four of four elements present - a number with units; a stated perturbation; an explicit alternative explanation with a way to rule it out; a delayed measurement. Missing any element means the practice plan cannot distinguish learning from momentary adjustment.
depth.summary: A skill is a reproducible change in performance measured on a task, not a substance in a structure. Any defensible skill claim names the component that changed (perceptual, model-based, command selection, or correction), the measurement that isolates it, and the comparison that rules out strategy, effort and luck. The textbook evidence distributes these components across cortical, basal ganglia and cerebellar circuits; the review evidence shows the systems have different time courses; and the after-effect logic shows how to demonstrate an internal change rather than a temporary accommodation. Transfer the framework to any new skill: identify what the performer now detects, predicts, decides and executes, and then ask which measurement would move if each of those changed. That question structure will carry into lesson 62, where the same discipline exposes the difference between a training study and an everyday plasticity claim.

lessons.title: Training-induced change and everyday plasticity claims are different kinds of evidence
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to say what kind of evidence a training study provides, what kind of evidence a correlational claim about everyday experience provides, and why the two are not interchangeable. A training study gives a person a controlled dose of practice and measures change on a task before and after, ideally against a control group. Its characteristic strengths are temporal order (the training comes first) and randomisation, which is what licenses the word 'caused'. Its characteristic weaknesses are that it can only speak about the task trained and about the people sampled, and that it can be confounded by expectancy and retest effects. An everyday plasticity claim - musicians have thicker auditory cortex, bilinguals switch tasks differently, meditators show different default-network activity - is usually a between-groups comparison with no randomisation. Its characteristic strength is ecological validity, since the experience really did happen. Its characteristic weakness is that the experience was not assigned, so training effects and pre-existing differences are entangled, and anyone who chose or succeeded in that experience may differ in many ways besides the experience. The vocabulary problem is that both literatures use the word 'plasticity' for change at the synaptic level, while the public claim is usually about benefit at the level of life outcomes. Those are separate questions. Neuroscience Online, Section 1, Chapter 7, sub-section 7.1 'Homosynaptic Plasticity' and 7.3 'Long-Term Potentiation' describe use-dependent synaptic change. That change is a mechanism; it does not tell you whether the resulting change helps the person, whether it is reversible, or whether it generalises to anything else. A depressing illustration of the gap is that the same mechanisms strengthen unwanted associations and maladaptive motor patterns. The review 'Cognitive Training: A Field in Search of a Phenomenon' states the transfer problem sharply: on its reading, the overall effect of far transfer is null, and the estimated effect from treatment versus active control is close to zero. 'Experts bodies, experts minds', a review of how physical and mental training shape the brain, is useful for the opposite reason: it documents the training-induced brain differences that do exist, and shows how many designs cannot distinguish the training from the selection of people who pursue it. Three qualifications complete the picture. First, near transfer usually does occur, because practising a task makes you better at that task: specificity is the expected result, not a disappointment. Second, 'no far transfer' is a claim about average effects in particular literatures, not a law banning every transfer in every design. Third, an old but instructive motor-learning result, published in 1997 by Shadmehr and Brashers-Krug (PMC6793707), showed that two conflicting force fields learned close together interfere, while the same fields learned a day apart do not. That is evidence for a consolidation process with a time window, from a small 1990s sample, and it should be cited with its era attached.
lessons.example: Compute three numbers that decide whether a training claim survives. First, effect size. Suppose the trained group improves 12 points on a task whose population standard deviation is 15 points. The standardised change is 12 divided by 15, which is 0.80 - a large effect on conventional benchmarks. Now suppose the same study measures an untrained task and finds a 2.25-point gain: 2.25 divided by 15 is 0.15, conventionally small. The arithmetic makes the transfer claim explicit: a large trained effect and a small untrained effect is a description of near transfer, and calling it 'cognitive improvement' shifts the claim to a level the data do not reach. Second, variance accounted for. A correlation between an experience and a brain or cognitive measure, with r = 0.30, corresponds to r-squared = 0.09, or nine per cent of the variance; r = 0.20 gives four per cent. Those figures are not an argument that the association is meaningless, but they show why a group difference on a scatterplot can look convincing while leaving most variation unexplained. Third, regression to the mean. If a study recruits people on the basis of a low score - a common design in cognitive-training research - and the test has a retest reliability of 0.70, a participant who scored one standard deviation below the mean is expected to move about (1 - 0.70) x 1.0 = 0.30 standard deviations toward the mean on retesting, roughly 4.5 points at a standard deviation of 15, before any treatment acts. Multiply by an inactive control that is expected to gain nothing and an active control that expects to gain a lot, and the design, not the training, can generate the headline. Read the arithmetic as a checklist: state the standardised change in the trained and untrained tasks separately, state the variance explained if the design is correlational, and state what an untreated group of equally selected participants would be expected to do.
lessons.question: A press release reports that six weeks of a training application raised the trained task score by 0.8 standard deviations and therefore improved 'general cognitive ability'. Which two design facts would most change how you read the claim?
lessons.answer: Whether there was an active control group with the same expectations, and whether the general-ability claim rests on a different, untrained outcome measure rather than on the trained task itself.
lessons.distractor: Whether the study lasted six weeks rather than twelve, since only longer training can produce general ability gains.
lessons.correction: Duration is a plausible secondary question, but the two facts that decide the interpretation are the comparison group and the outcome measure. An inactive or waiting-list control leaves expectancy, retest practice and regression to the mean unaddressed, and expectancy can be substantial in a task that participants know is meant to make them smarter, which is why the placebo-control literature recommends active controls and measured expectations. The second fact is the level of the outcome: 0.8 standard deviations on the trained task is a near-transfer result compatible with simply getting better at that task, whereas a general-ability claim needs an untrained battery with an independent administration. Without both facts, the release has restated the design as a benefit.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: random allocation assigns participants to conditions by chance, which balances unknown confounders on average; an active control performs a plausible, engaging activity so that expectation and effort are similar across arms; an inactive control does something minimal or nothing; near transfer is improvement on a task similar to the trained one; far transfer is improvement on a dissimilar task or on a broad ability; a retest effect is improvement caused by having taken the test before; regression to the mean is the statistical tendency of extreme scores to move toward the average on retesting; self-selection means participants chose the condition or the expertise. Also distinguish within-person change (the same people measured twice) from between-person difference (two groups measured once). Most everyday plasticity claims are the second kind, and they cannot be re-described as the first without a design that follows people over time.
depth.mechanism: Why is near transfer expected while far transfer is not? Practice builds representations specific to the practised material: the perceptual features you learned to discriminate, the motor sequence you learned to issue, and the retrieval routes you used. Improvement is thus carried by those specific representations, and a new task that requires different features recruits different representations, so the benefit does not travel. Far transfer would require something else - a shared capacity such as working memory - to have been raised, or a strategy that is genuinely task-general to have been acquired. Both are possible in principle, which is why far-transfer research exists, but the effect must be demonstrated on untrained measures against a control, and the systematic reviews of training against active controls report estimates near zero. The correlational literature has a different mechanism problem: selection. People who practise music for ten years differ from non-musicians in age of start, family resources, personality, hearing, and sustained attention, and any of these could produce the measured brain difference. Longitudinal designs help only partly, since the decision to continue is itself a variable. Note too what a synaptic-level mechanism can and cannot carry. LTP at a synapse is evidence that a circuit can change with use; it is silent on whether the change is adaptive, how it interacts with other changes, and what it does to a life outcome. Keeping the levels separate is not pedantry: it is the only way to know what additional measurement a claim requires.
depth.secondExample: Take a contrasting worked application from adult skill acquisition outside the laboratory. A hospital introduces a simulation curriculum for central-line insertion and reports that complication rates fall. The comparison here is institutional, not randomised: the same unit before and after, with no active control and no way to rule out concurrent changes in staffing, equipment or case mix. Apply the checklist. What is the trained outcome? Insertion performance on a simulator - near transfer, expected to improve. What is the claimed outcome? Patient complications - a different measure at a different level, plausibly connected but subject to many other causes, and susceptible to measurement change such as more careful reporting after a new curriculum. What would strengthen the claim? A comparison unit, an objective outcome definition fixed in advance, and a measure of whether the trained skill was actually performed in the ward. Notice that this is a case where the intervention is worth doing even though the evidence is weak; the epistemic point is not 'do nothing' but 'state what the evidence supports'. That distinction - usefulness of an intervention versus strength of a causal claim - recurs in lesson 69 when we compare pharmacological and behavioural trials.
depth.mistake: The misconception to retire is 'the brain changed, therefore the training worked'. Brain change is a mechanism-level observation and can accompany improvement, effort, novelty, fatigue or measurement noise. Its reverse is equally common: 'there was no transfer, therefore nothing was learned'. Specific practice does produce robust learning, and specificity is the normal finding in skill research rather than evidence of failure. A third error is treating a group difference in structure or activity as if it came from training simply because the training is easy to imagine. Ask instead what the non-trained comparison would have looked like, and whether anyone who could not have chosen the experience was included in the comparison. A practical diagnostic: whenever a sentence contains 'rewires the brain' or 'boosts', replace it with the specific measured change and see whether the sentence still means anything.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Find one news article that reports a training or experience effect on the brain. Write a four-line audit: (1) the measured outcome and its units, and whether it was trained or untrained; (2) the comparison condition, or the absence of one; (3) the alternative explanations left open, named specifically (expectancy, retest, regression to the mean, selection); (4) one sentence that the study could support, written without the words boost, rewire, or enhance. Model response: 'Outcome: reaction time in a switching task, trained variant, milliseconds, n = 42. Comparison: waiting list only; no expectation measure. Open explanations: retest practice of about 0.3 SD expected, plus expectancy. Supportable sentence: participants who practised the switching game became faster at that game over six weeks; the study does not show faster thinking in general.' Self-review rubric: the audit scores four points if it names a unit, identifies whether the measure was trained, names at least two specific alternatives, and rewrites the claim with the same scope as the evidence. Score two additional points for stating what a stronger design would add.
depth.summary: Training studies and everyday-experience correlations answer different questions, and neither can be converted into the other by enthusiasm. Randomised training supports a causal claim about the trained task, bounded by expectancy, retest and regression artefacts; correlational expertise research supports a difference that selection can explain. Synaptic-level evidence of plasticity is a mechanism, not a benefit, and it neither forbids nor guarantees transfer. The working tools are standardised changes computed separately for trained and untrained tasks, variance explained stated honestly, an explicit active control, and a written statement of what the study could support. Lesson 63 puts the same discipline to a case where the evidence is genuinely strong but frequently overstated in public: critical and sensitive periods in vision and language.

lessons.title: Critical periods revisited: what vision and language evidence actually constrains
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to state what a critical period is, distinguish it from a sensitive period, and explain what the vision and language literatures do and do not establish. A critical period is a developmental window during which a particular experience has a large and lasting effect and after which the same experience has much less effect. A sensitive period is the weaker claim: the effect is larger earlier but not absent later. The distinction matters because the two words get swapped in public argument, and almost all the human evidence supports the weaker claim. The canonical case comes from vision. The review 'Critical periods in amblyopia' (Hensch and Quinlan) states that the shift in ocular dominance of binocular neurons induced by monocular deprivation is the canonical model of synaptic plasticity confined to a postnatal critical period, and it traces the definition to Wiesel and Hubel in 1963 - animal work from the 1960s and 1970s, on cats and monkeys, which should always be cited with that era attached. The same review shows how much the field has moved: ocular dominance was originally defined as a change in the spiking output of primary visual cortex neurons, whereas current work measures visually evoked synaptic potentials, intrinsic haemodynamic signals, immediate early gene activation, and the morphology of thalamocortical axons and dendritic spines. Its section headings are a map of the modern argument: inhibition and critical period induction, molecular reactivation of critical period in adulthood, environmental reactivation in adulthood, and reactivating plasticity to enhance recovery. In other words, the contemporary literature is largely about reopening, not only about closing. Language supplies a competing case. The paper 'Rethinking the critical period for language' reviews evidence from American Sign Language and is unusually explicit about scope, with sections titled Points of Agreement and What We Did Not Claim; it argues that the age at which learners first gain access to a language predicts later grammatical outcome, while the explanation involves the language environment and the measurement of language, not age alone. 'The Critical Period Hypothesis in Second Language Acquisition: A Statistical Critique and a Reanalysis' takes the same question from the statistical side and shows how conclusions about nonlinearity depend on modelling choices: how age of arrival is entered, whether age at testing is partialled out, how aptitude is estimated, and whether quadratic terms are justified. Neuroscience Online, Section 4, Chapter 8, sub-section 8.2, 'Is Language Innate or Learned', shows that the underlying debate is old and partly conceptual. Three qualifications follow. First, animal models dominate the mechanistic evidence, and the bridge to human development requires assumptions about comparability. Second, individual variability within an age group is usually larger than the average difference between age groups, which is why windows describe averages, not fates. Third, the metaphor itself is doing work in education and policy that the data do not carry: 'the window closed' is a claim about the average effect of an experience, not a statement that learning is impossible.
lessons.example: Two numerical exercises show why apparently simple age effects are fragile. First, take a hypothetical study reporting a proficiency decline of 2.5 points per year of age of arrival on a 100-point test whose standard deviation is 15. Across ages of arrival from 3 to 13 - a span of 10 years - the fitted decline is 10 x 2.5 = 25 points, and 25 divided by 15 is 1.67 standard deviations. That is a large average difference, large enough to be visible in almost any sample. Now check whether the test can even express it at the older end. If the test has a practical ceiling of about 95 points and the late-arrival group's mean is 80, the available headroom is 95 minus 80, or 15 points, which is 1.00 standard deviation. A true difference of 1.67 standard deviations cannot be observed on a measure that leaves room for only 1.00, so the measured gap understates the difference, compresses the distribution of late learners into a narrow band, and biases any estimate of where a breakpoint falls. This is a censoring problem, and it is one reason the reanalysis paper criticises breakpoint estimation. Second, attrition. Suppose 30 per cent of the late-arrival group drops out and those who leave score on average 0.50 standard deviations below the group mean. Removing them shifts the retained group's mean upward by the dropout proportion times their deviation, 0.30 x 0.50 = 0.15 standard deviations, which at a standard deviation of 15 points is 2.25 points. A 2.25-point shift is small, but it is systematic: it works in the direction that makes late acquisition look better, and it compounds if attrition is selective for other reasons. The arithmetic does not show that sensitive periods are unreal. It shows that the width and location of a window are estimated from measures that can hide exactly the differences the window is supposed to explain.
lessons.question: A parent asks whether a ten-year-old has permanently missed the window for learning a second language. Which answer is best supported by the human evidence reviewed in this lesson?
lessons.answer: Age of first exposure predicts average outcomes in several studies, particularly for grammar and for learners without earlier language access, but the evidence supports a graded sensitive period rather than a closed window, so a ten-year-old can still reach high proficiency and outcomes vary widely within every starting age.
lessons.distractor: The window is closed for grammar after roughly age seven, so the child can still learn vocabulary but will never acquire grammar natively; teaching effort is therefore better spent elsewhere.
lessons.correction: That answer states a hard cut-off that the literature does not support. The three reading sources converge on a more careful claim. The American Sign Language review is explicit that age of first language access shapes later grammatical outcomes while declining to claim that a specific age closes the door, and the statistical critique shows that the apparent sharpness of the age function depends on modelling decisions and on measures that compress the outcome space at the older end, which is exactly why breakpoints are hard to estimate. What the evidence does support is a graded effect: earlier exposure, on average, produces better outcomes on demanding grammatical measures, with wide overlap between age groups. Practical consequence: the honest answer reports an average tendency with variability, not a verdict on a particular child, and it does not convert a population-level gradient into a prohibition.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: monocular deprivation is the reduction of input to one eye; ocular dominance refers to the relative response of a binocular neuron or region to the two eyes; amblyopia is reduced vision in an eye not explained by structural damage to the eye itself and is described in this literature as a developmental consequence of abnormal early visual experience; deprivation means reduced or absent input, while privation is the extreme form. A critical period is a window with a large and lasting effect of experience; a sensitive period is a window with a stronger but not exclusive effect. Age of arrival (AoA) is the age at which a learner begins acquiring a language in the environment where it is spoken; age of first language access refers to a deaf learner's first exposure to an accessible language, such as a sign language, which is conceptually different from learning a second language after a first is established. Ultimate attainment means the highest level a learner reaches rather than performance on a single test occasion.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms are usually offered and they are not the same claim. The first is competitive wiring: early experience determines which inputs win the competition for cortical territory, so deprivation of one eye gives the other a durable advantage, and the mature circuit is stable because the losing inputs have been pruned. The second is a brake on plasticity: as circuits mature, factors such as changes in excitatory and inhibitory balance, the maturation of inhibitory interneuron circuits, the accumulation of extracellular matrix structures around some neurons, and myelination-related signalling reduce the capacity for change. The review you are reading is organised around the second framework, since its sections progress from inhibition and the induction of the period through molecular and environmental reactivation to recovery. The distinction matters for prediction. A competitive-wiring account predicts that the deficit reflects which inputs won; a brake account predicts that the deficit can be partially reversed if the brake can be released, which is why adult recovery experiments are even interesting. Limitations: most of the causal evidence comes from non-human animals with experimental deprivation, human evidence is largely observational and confounded by environment and assessment, and the bridge from a species with a different visual system and lifespan requires argument rather than assumption. Human critical period claims should therefore be made in the weaker, graded form unless the specific human design justifies more.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the visual case with the language case to see how differently the same vocabulary is earned. In visual development the manipulation is direct and extreme - close an eye during a defined developmental window and observe the consequence - so the causal structure is clear in animals and the human evidence is a scaled-down analogy involving amblyopia treatment. In language acquisition you cannot assign a child's first language. The strongest human designs are therefore natural experiments of circumstance: deaf learners who received an accessible sign language at different ages, and immigrants whose age at arrival varies. These designs have the causal structure of a natural experiment but confounds you cannot remove - family circumstances, language of instruction, amount of exposure, and the very measurement of proficiency. Now consider a prediction the two cases make differently. If plasticity were simply turned off on schedule, an adult learning a second language would show near-zero gains and no neural response to training; the training literature shows substantial adult learning, with lower average ultimate attainment in some domains rather than absence of learning. If instead plasticity is graded by circuit and by demand, you would expect large age effects precisely where fine timing and high-fidelity sensory mapping matter, and smaller effects where explicit, slow, feedback-rich learning can substitute. That pattern is roughly what the human evidence shows, and it is a graded-sensitive-period prediction rather than a critical-period one.
depth.mistake: The error to retire is the closed-window inference: 'research shows that a critical period ends at age X, so learning after that is futile'. It is a diagnostic error when a claim moves from an average group difference to a statement about an individual, and from a hard interpretation of a model to a hard fact about a person. The correction has three parts. First, models with nonlinear terms are fitted to noisy data, and their breakpoints are estimates with wide uncertainty that depend on modelling choices such as entering age linearly or quadratically and partialling out age at testing. Second, many measures compress high performers at the ceiling, so the older learners appear more similar to one another than they are. Third, the appropriate inference from an average gradient is a probabilistic one about a population, not a categorical one about the learner in front of you. A related error on the other side is dismissing sensitive periods entirely because the effects are statistical: a well-replicated average advantage for early exposure on demanding grammatical measures is a real finding even when no window slams shut.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Find one public claim about age and learning - an advertisement, a policy document, a news article, or a course description. Produce a three-part analysis in under 200 words. (1) Quote or paraphrase the claim and classify it as critical-period or sensitive-period in its wording. (2) Identify which measurement could not support the claim: a cross-sectional group difference, a fitted breakpoint without an uncertainty interval, a ceiling-limited outcome, or a measure of the wrong construct. (3) Rewrite the claim in a form the evidence could support, with a stated population and an average-effect verb. Model response: 'Claim: languages must be learned before seven or the accent is permanent. Classification: critical period in wording. Cannot be supported by: a cross-sectional accent-rating study with listener raters and no measure of first exposure age or exposure quantity. Rewrite: in samples of learners measured this way, average accent ratings were closer to native for earlier starters, with substantial overlap between groups and wide variation within every starting age.' Self-review rubric: one point for correct classification, two for naming a specific measurement problem from this lesson, two for a rewrite that keeps the original population and uses an average-effect verb. A rewrite that says 'earlier exposure always helps' loses a point for overreach in the other direction.
depth.summary: Critical period is the strong claim; sensitive period is the claim the human evidence usually supports. Vision supplies the canonical animal model and a modern literature organised around reopening plasticity as much as closing it; language supplies natural experiments that support graded age effects on demanding grammatical measures while remaining vulnerable to censoring, selective attrition and modelling choices. The durable lesson is methodological: before accepting any age-window claim, ask what was measured, how the outcome was bounded, who left the sample, and whether a breakpoint was fitted and with what uncertainty. Lesson 64 applies the same scrutiny to a case with far more public visibility and far weaker mechanistic grounding: adolescent brain development.

lessons.title: Adolescent brain development: what the imaging shows, and what the 'immature brake' story adds
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to name what each common developmental imaging measure actually indexes, restate the dual-systems model in a testable form, and say why its popular version outruns its evidence. Start with the measures. A structural MRI volume is an estimate of tissue boundaries from a mathematical model, not a count of cells. Cortical thickness derived from the same images changes with age, but the change can reflect myelination at the inner boundary, synaptic reorganisation, or the geometry of the surface reconstruction, and the measures used in large developmental samples are not interchangeable with the ones used in animal studies of synapse elimination. Diffusion MRI indices such as fractional anisotropy are sensitive to the restriction of water diffusion by tissue microstructure; they are often summarised in prose as evidence of 'myelination', which is an interpretation rather than the measurement, since several microstructural features move the index. Task functional MRI measures a haemodynamic correlate of local activity, so a group difference in a limbic or prefrontal region is a difference in a blood-oxygen signal during a task, not a readout of the strength of a control system. These are not pedantic distinctions. The dual-systems model is a claim about the relationship between two psychological constructs, sensation seeking and self-regulation, and their neural substrates. The review 'The dual systems model: Review, reappraisal, and reaffirmation' states the position and its psychological manifestation terms, and it reports evidence that sensation seeking peaks earlier than self-regulation develops; its own final section lists unresolved questions. The critique 'Arrested development? Reconsidering dual-systems models' argues that the framing - a ventral affective system conferring vulnerability plus a prefrontal control system buffering it - is an intuitive account that pervades many fields, and it shows evidence of complexity in adolescent brain-behaviour relationships, with a caution box on why the models are so potent and another on updating the interpretive toolkit. 'Mind the gap' attacks the statistical implementation: how the imbalance is measured, whether growth mixture models and latent difference score models support a single developmental pattern, and whether the imbalance construct as operationalised is specific enough to test. Three qualifications follow. First, the metaphors do real explanatory work and are therefore hard to retire: an accelerator-and-brakes image feels like an explanation while making no quantitative prediction. Second, cross-sectional age differences and longitudinal within-person change give different pictures, so 'the trajectory' depends on the design. Third, the population-level claim cannot be applied to an individual teenager, whose own variation dwarfs the group difference.
lessons.example: Run three numbers against a typical dual-systems headline, which claims that limbic reactivity rises and prefrontal control lags, producing an imbalance that causes risk taking. First, variance explained. Suppose the correlation between a reward-reactivity index and a real-world risk-taking measure in a developmental sample is 0.20. Squaring gives 0.04, or four per cent of variance. A scatterplot with a fitted line and a wide confidence band is fully compatible with that figure, and it is far less impressive than the phrase 'limbic reactivity predicts risk taking' implies. Second, attenuation by unreliable difference scores. The imbalance is usually computed as a difference or ratio between a reactivity measure and a control measure. If each component is measured with reliability 0.70, the difference score's reliability is lower, and an observed correlation equals the true correlation multiplied by the square root of the reliability of each measure. Take a conservative difference-score reliability of 0.45 and a true correlation of 0.30: the expected observed correlation is 0.30 x 0.671 = 0.20, exactly the value in the headline above. The headline therefore may not be evidence that adolescents have a small imbalance effect; it may be evidence that the construct was measured with limited precision. Third, sample size. Detecting a correlation of 0.20 with 80 per cent power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 requires roughly 194 participants, before allowing for missing imaging data and exclusions. A neuroimaging study with 30 adolescents per group has very little chance of estimating that association precisely, and its significant result, if any, is likely to be an overestimate. The arithmetic does not refute the dual-systems account; it specifies what a test of it must report: the reliability of the imbalance measure, the variance explained, the design (longitudinal or cross-sectional) and an adequately powered sample.
lessons.question: A news article reports that 'the adolescent brain's emotional centre matures years before the reasoning centre, so teenagers cannot control their impulses'. Which single change would most improve the article's relationship to the evidence?
lessons.answer: Replacing the claim about an internal imbalance with a measured, longitudinal association between a specific task-based index and a specific behaviour, reported with its strength and its between-person variability.
lessons.distractor: Adding the average age at which prefrontal development completes, because the article's problem is that it left out the exact age of maturation.
lessons.correction: Supplying a number would make the article more precise without making it more defensible. The central problem is that the article asserts a causal, individual-level mechanism from group-average structural differences and never states the strength of the association or how much people vary. A measured longitudinal association with a named index and a reported effect size is falsifiable: it can be shown to be weak, to be specific to one task, or to be no larger than measurement unreliability allows. Adding an age of maturation is worse than useless, because it converts a contested average trajectory estimate into a factual deadline, which is precisely the overreach the critiques in this lesson identify.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: adolescence is defined behaviourally and socially, typically as the period from puberty to adult role transitions, so samples are defined by age in imaging studies and the boundaries are conventions. Cortical thickness and cortical surface area are two separately computed structural metrics; they change with different age patterns and should not be treated as one measure of maturation. Fractional anisotropy is a diffusion MRI index; mean diffusivity is another. BOLD stands for blood-oxygen-level-dependent and indexes a haemodynamic response. A construct is a psychological or neural variable inferred from measurements, such as self-regulation. Reliability is the consistency of a measurement across repetitions; attenuation is the reduction in observed correlation caused by unreliable measurement. An imbalance score is a difference or ratio between two constructs. A latent difference score model estimates change between occasions as a latent variable; growth mixture modelling identifies subgroups with different trajectory shapes.
depth.mechanism: Why might two systems develop at different rates, and what would that require? The account requires at least three things: that reward-related circuits show heightened responsiveness around puberty, plausibly linked to changes in the dopamine system and in the gonadal hormone environment; that cognitive-control circuitry and its connections continue to develop across adolescence, which longitudinal structural and functional work broadly supports as a gradual process; and a mechanism by which the mismatch produces behaviour, which is where the model is weakest, because a group-level difference in two trajectories is not automatically a dynamic interaction within a person. The statistical critiques in this lesson attack exactly that gap. A within-person imbalance requires measurement of both components in the same people on several occasions, a defensible operationalisation of imbalance (difference, ratio, or interaction term), and enough occasions to estimate individual trajectories. Most published tests compare group means or fit a single growth curve to all participants, which cannot show that people with the largest imbalance are the people who take the most risks. The neuroimaging add-on has its own limit: task BOLD differences between age groups can reflect performance differences, effort, strategy, head motion correlated with age, and how the data were modelled, all of which can masquerade as developmental change in a control system.
depth.secondExample: Apply the same scrutiny to a behavioural claim in the opposite direction, to see that the problem is not specific to brain imaging. A large literature reports that adolescents take more risks when peers are present, measured in laboratory driving and decision tasks; and population data show a rise in some risk behaviours in late adolescence and early adulthood. It is tempting to read both as one phenomenon. But compare the measurements. The laboratory task measures a choice under observation on a single occasion, with a payoff structure the experimenter defined. The population statistic aggregates events with heterogeneous reporting, and it is confounded by exposure: teenagers and young adults drive more, work in riskier jobs, and have different supervision. Neither measure is wrong, and neither converts into the other. The productive move is to ask what pattern both would predict. If peer presence specifically amplifies reward sensitivity, the laboratory effect should be largest in tasks with immediate, social rewards and should interact with individual differences in reward responsiveness; if instead the population data reflect exposure, the age pattern should shift when exposure changes, which it has for some behaviours as driving patterns and licensing rules changed. Testing those predictions is how a developmental claim becomes falsifiable. Notice that this exercise uses the lesson's measure-first discipline and requires no imaging at all.
depth.mistake: The diagnostic error is the car metaphor treated as a finding: 'a powerful accelerator with an immature brake'. It feels explanatory while predicting nothing, and it misstates the anatomy, since the constructs are not two peripheral devices but distributed systems whose interactions are the scientific question. Its practical error is that it licenses individual-level conclusions from group-level averages, and it often implies that risk taking in adolescence is a biological inevitability, which is contradicted by variation between individuals and between cultures with different opportunity structures. A second, related error is treating an age at which a trajectory 'matures', such as 25, as a documented switch point; such numbers are usually where an average curve flattens by convention, estimated with wide bands, and reported without uncertainty in the popular retelling. A third error is believing that a difference in the direction predicted by the model counts as strong evidence for it. A soft prediction can be satisfied by many mechanisms; support requires specificity, which means showing that a competing account such as effort, exposure, strategy or motion does not explain the same pattern.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Design, on paper, a study that could support or embarrass the dual-systems account, in at most 250 words. Include: the two constructs and the exact task or measure for each; the imbalance definition (difference score, latent interaction, or within-person coupling across occasions); the number of measurement occasions; the predicted pattern in within-person terms; and one competing explanation you will measure and rule out. Model response: 'Construct 1, reward responsiveness: a monetary reward anticipation task, with mean BOLD contrast in a reward-related region defined a priori plus a behavioural choice measure; construct 2, self-regulation: a validated self-report scale and a stop-signal task. Imbalance: within-person standardised difference, computed per occasion, with reliability reported for each component and for the difference. Occasions: four, at annual intervals. Prediction: participants whose imbalance scores are larger than their own average should show more risk taking in the periods that follow, controlling for age. Competing explanation measured: head motion and sleep, since both correlate with age and with task performance.' Self-review rubric: two points for naming an imbalance statistic and committing to reporting its reliability; two for within-person, temporally ordered predictions; two for identifying a specific confound and how it will be measured; one point for stating what result would count against the account.
depth.summary: Developmental imaging measures microstructural and haemodynamic indices, not maturity or control capacity, and each index has several interpretations. The dual-systems model is a specific psychological claim whose popular form - an immature brake - is unfalsifiable and individually overreaching, while its rigorous form remains an open question that requires within-person imbalance measures, reliable difference scores, adequate samples and controls for motion and effort. Group-average trajectories, cross-sectional and longitudinal designs, and population statistics answer different questions and cannot be merged by rhetoric. Carry forward the measure-first discipline: whenever a developmental claim names a system, ask which measurement moved, in whose data, and by how much. Lesson 65 takes the same question into ageing, where the practical stakes of mixing normal change with disease are highest.

lessons.title: Ageing: separating normal cognitive change from disease, and why the boundary is a measurement decision
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to describe what normal cognitive ageing looks like in longitudinal data, explain why categorical diagnoses and continuous measures tell different stories, and compute what a test result means at different base rates. Begin with what normal ageing actually is in the best available data. The study 'Trajectories of normal cognitive aging' compares three kinds of comparison: cross-sectional (different people at different ages tested once), longitudinal (the same people followed over years), and quasi-longitudinal (people of different birth cohorts tested once without prior test experience). Its summary is that normal cognitive ageing is characterised by nearly linear declines from early adulthood in speed and accelerating declines in memory and reasoning, while vocabulary knowledge increased until the decade of the sixties in all three comparisons. Crucially, the age trends in the quasi-longitudinal comparisons more closely resembled the cross-sectional comparisons than the longitudinal ones, which points to cohort differences - education, health, technology, test familiarity - being folded into any single-occasion age comparison. That is why a cross-sectional 'decline with age' curve is a claim about the average difference between people born decades apart, not about change within a person. Now the classification problem. 'Cognitive Aging and Dementia: A Life Span Perspective' lays out the epidemiology and then devotes its later sections to categorical versus continuous models of cognitive ageing and dementia, to person-to-person heterogeneity in the rate, shape and timing of decline, and to interpreting the correlates of adult cognitive function for the purpose of what it calls a change-based assessment of dementia. Its point is structural: dementia is a clinical syndrome defined by decline plus functional consequence, whereas the measures that predict it - cognitive test scores, imaging, biomarkers - are continuous, noisy and often partly independent of function. Neuroscience Online, Section 4, Chapter 10, opens with 10.1, 'Aging Is a Normal Biological Process', then moves to 10.3 'Alzheimer's Disease', 10.4 'Diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease' and 10.9 'Role of Risk Factors and the Environment'. Read that chapter with its date in mind: it predates current biomarker-based research frameworks, so its diagnostic sections are useful for the logic of classification and the history of the categories, not as a statement of present practice. Three qualifications follow. First, a diagnosis is a decision made for a purpose - clinical care, research inclusion, insurance - and each purpose needs different thresholds. Second, many people carry substantial pathology and perform normally, and many who meet a dementia criterion have mixed pathology rather than one clean cause, which is why continuous and categorical models coexist. Third, an individual's own variability across occasions is often as large as the difference between the average seventy-year-old and the average eighty-year-old, so single measurements support weak inferences. This lesson is education about how such measurements are interpreted; it is not clinical advice, and any personal concern belongs with a qualified clinician.
lessons.example: Three calculations make the boundary between normal and pathological concrete. First, what counts as real change in one person. Suppose a memory test has a population standard deviation of 15 points and a retest reliability of 0.85. The standard error of measurement is the standard deviation multiplied by the square root of one minus the reliability: 15 x square root of 0.15 = 15 x 0.387 = 5.81 points. A change would have to exceed roughly 1.96 times that standard error, about 11.4 points, before it comfortably exceeds test noise in a single person. A drop of 5 points, commonly reported as 'decline', is inside the noise band. Second, what a score means at a given base rate. Take a test with 90 per cent sensitivity and 90 per cent specificity and a population in which 5 per cent have the condition. In 1,000 people: 50 have the condition and 45 of them test positive; of the 950 who do not, 95 test positive. Positive results total 140, so the chance that a positive result belongs to someone with the condition is 45/140 = 32.1 per cent. Repeat with a 1 per cent base rate - the situation for a young adult screened opportunistically: 10 cases, 9 detected, and 99 false positives among 990, giving 9/108 = 8.3 per cent. Repeat with a 20 per cent base rate, as in a specialist memory clinic: 200 cases, 180 detected, 80 false positives, so 180/260 = 69.2 per cent. The test never changed; the meaning of a positive result changed by a factor of eight. Third, express a difference in standard deviation units instead of points. A two-point difference on a 30-point screening instrument whose standard deviation is 3 is 0.67 standard deviations - moderate. The same two points on a 100-point instrument with a standard deviation of 15 is 0.13 standard deviations - small. Always convert before you react to a number.
lessons.question: A 74-year-old scores below a published cut-off on a brief cognitive screen during a routine appointment. According to the reasoning in this lesson, what is the most defensible interpretation?
lessons.answer: The result raises the probability that further assessment is warranted and cannot be interpreted as a diagnosis, because a single below-cut-off score is one noisy measurement whose meaning depends on base rate, retest reliability, education and prior level, and on whether function is affected.
lessons.distractor: The result means the person has cognitive impairment, because published cut-offs are calibrated so that people below them meet the clinical criterion.
lessons.correction: Cut-offs set on a single occasion cannot deliver a diagnosis, and the arithmetic shows why. At a low base rate, most positive results are false positives even at 90 per cent sensitivity and specificity; a single measurement has a noise band of roughly plus or minus 11 points when the standard deviation is 15 and reliability is 0.85; and a below-cut-off score can reflect education, language, hearing, mood, sleep, medication effects or simple test inexperience rather than disease. A diagnosis is a decision that combines a change from the person's own earlier level, functional consequences, and context, and it belongs to a qualified clinician. The lesson's point is about inference: a screen changes probabilities and prompts the next, better measurement; it does not classify a person.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: normal ageing is a statistical description of typical change in a population, not a value judgement or a guarantee for any individual. A clinical syndrome is a defined pattern of signs, symptoms and functional consequences; a pathology is a tissue-level process; a biomarker is a measurable indicator associated with a process, which may or may not be causal. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who test positive; specificity is the proportion without it who test negative; positive predictive value is the proportion of positive results that belong to people with the condition, and it depends on prevalence. Reliable change is a change larger than the measurement's own error. Cognitive reserve is a hypothesis that some life experiences allow people to tolerate more pathology before showing functional impairment. Cohort effects are differences between people born in different eras, which contaminate cross-sectional age comparisons. Mild cognitive impairment is an intermediate category that some people later re-enter the normal range from, which is one reason the category is debated.
depth.mechanism: What changes with age, and why is there no single mechanism? Several processes advance together and partly independently: reductions in processing speed, which plausibly reflect widespread changes in neural conduction and synaptic efficacy rather than a single lesion; declines in the efficiency of episodic memory retrieval and in executive control; vascular changes that affect white-matter integrity; and in some people the accumulation of protein aggregates and inflammatory processes that define neurodegenerative disease. Because the contributors are multiple and correlated with age, any single measure is a summary of many processes, and two people of the same age can have quite different profiles. The categorical-continuous problem follows directly. A threshold applied to a continuous, multi-causal quantity will produce categories whose members differ from one another, and whose boundaries move when the threshold, the test or the base rate moves. This is not a reason to abandon categories: clinical decisions require them. It is a reason to treat a category label as the output of a decision rule applied to measurements, and to ask what rule, applied to what measurement, in what population. It also explains why predictive claims are weaker than they look: a biomarker that is associated with a disease process in a population can be common in people who never develop the syndrome, so a positive biomarker result shifts probabilities without determining outcomes.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the clinical-classification problem with a research-design problem that uses the same measurements, to see how the purpose changes the rule. Suppose a laboratory wants to detect a treatment effect on cognitive decline in healthy older adults over two years. The classification question disappears: no participant receives a diagnosis, and the outcome is a continuous change score. Now the arithmetic changes character. The relevant question is whether a change can be measured precisely enough to be seen, which depends on retest reliability, practice effects, and the variance of change across people. If the standard error of measurement is about 5.8 points on a scale with a standard deviation of 15, a treatment effect of 2 points is smaller than any individual's measurement noise, so the study must estimate a group mean difference with a sample large enough that the standard error of the mean falls well below 2 points - which means many participants, and careful procedures to make the retest conditions constant. Notice the contrast with the diagnostic case: there, noise in one person was fatal to interpretation; here, noise can be averaged out across participants, and the design's power, not the individual's certainty, becomes the binding constraint. Same measure, different rule, because the purpose differs. That is the transferable insight of this lesson.
depth.mistake: Three errors are worth diagnosing precisely. The first is 'forgetting names is early dementia'. Word-finding difficulty increases with normal ageing, and a single forgetful episode is not evidence of a neurodegenerative process; the informative pattern is a decline from the person's own baseline that affects function, not a lapse. The second is 'everyone declines the same way'. Person-to-person heterogeneity in rate, shape and timing is a documented feature of these data, and vocabulary often holds or improves into the sixties and beyond, so an average decline curve is not a schedule. The third, and the one this lesson most wants you to catch, is 'a positive biomarker means the disease is coming'. A biomarker associated with a pathology at group level does not determine an individual's trajectory, both because many people with the pathology remain cognitively normal and because the syndrome requires functional consequences. The diagnostic correction is always the same: replace the categorical claim with the decision rule, the measurement, and the population to which it was applied.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Write a 200-word assessment plan for a fictional research question: does a two-year exercise programme slow cognitive decline in adults aged 65 to 80? Specify the outcome measure and its reliability, the retest interval and how practice effects will be handled, the analysis of change (and whether a categorical outcome such as incident impairment will be reported as well), and a statement of what the study cannot conclude. Model response: 'Primary outcome: composite episodic memory score, reported in standard deviation units; test-retest reliability from the published manual used to compute the standard error of measurement and the reliable-change threshold. Interval: baseline, 12 months, 24 months, with the same tester, same time of day, and alternate forms to reduce practice effects. Analysis: mixed model of change with baseline score, education and sex as covariates, reporting the standardised effect and its confidence interval; incident impairment reported separately as a secondary, categorical outcome with its base rate stated. Cannot conclude: that the programme prevents dementia, or that an individual participant's score change is clinically meaningful.' Self-review rubric: two points for specifying reliability and the reliable-change threshold; two for handling practice effects explicitly; two for stating a design-appropriate analysis with uncertainty; two for stating at least one thing the study cannot conclude.
depth.summary: Normal cognitive ageing is best described from longitudinal data as near-linear declines in speed and accelerating declines in memory and reasoning, with vocabulary often preserved, while single-occasion age comparisons carry cohort differences. Dementia is a syndrome requiring decline plus functional consequence; the measures that predict it are continuous and noisy; and the boundary between normal and pathological is a decision rule whose meaning depends on base rate, reliability and purpose. A positive screen shifts probabilities rather than naming a condition, and the practical consequence for reading claims is always to ask what rule was applied, to what measurement, in what population, for what purpose. Lesson 66 turns to a mechanism-level claim whose scientific status is genuinely unsettled - memory reconsolidation - and shows how to teach and cite a contested literature honestly.
