questions.prompt: Two experimenters train participants on a reaching task with a robot-applied sideways force. Experimenter A reports that trajectories became straight again after 300 trials and concludes that an internal model changed. Experimenter B reports that when the force is removed the hand now veers in the opposite direction. Which report supports the internal-model conclusion, and what does the other one show?
questions.answer: Experimenter B's after-effect supports the internal-model conclusion, because a reversed error after the perturbation is removed cannot be produced by a deliberate strategy; A's straight trajectories are equally consistent with a strategy of pushing sideways to cancel the force.
questions.distractor: Experimenter A's report is the stronger evidence, because a straight trajectory requires a precise internal prediction while an after-effect is only a transient error.
questions.correction: The logic turns on what each measurement excludes. Straight trajectories during the perturbation can be achieved by any successful correction, including an explicit, deliberate one, so they do not distinguish a changed internal model from a strategy. The after-effect excludes the strategy explanation: once the force is gone there is nothing to correct against, so a reversal in the opposite direction can only come from a prediction that is now wrong. The distractor inverts the inference: precision during a perturbation is a statement about performance, while the after-effect is a statement about the content of the prediction. This distinction is the operational core of lesson 61 and of the adaptation section of the review on multiple systems for motor skill learning.

questions.prompt: A trial reports that a six-week training programme produced a gain of 0.7 standard deviations on the trained task and 0.1 standard deviations on an untrained reasoning battery, with a waiting-list control. A commentary concludes that the programme improves cognition generally. Using the arithmetic of this unit, what is the strongest reading?
questions.answer: The two standardised changes describe near transfer only: 0.7 in the trained task against 0.1 in an untrained measure is the expected specificity pattern, and the waiting-list control leaves expectancy, retest and regression to the mean unaddressed.
questions.distractor: The pattern supports general improvement, because a positive change on the untrained battery in the same participants shows the benefit travelled beyond the trained task.
questions.correction: A small positive change in an untrained measure is not zero transfer, but it must be interpreted against what the control group and the measurement itself would produce. With a waiting-list control there is no comparison condition that matches expectancy, engagement or retest practice, and a 0.1 standard deviation change is well within the range these artefacts generate, particularly when participants were recruited on low baseline scores, where regression to the mean is expected to move scores toward the average. The commentary's claim also jumps levels: from a change in a task score to a change in general cognition, which would require an untrained battery administered independently and compared with an active control. Lesson 62 supplies exactly this checklist; compare with the near-zero transfer-versus-active-control estimates in the review on cognitive training.

questions.prompt: A study finds that children who received an accessible sign language before age three outperform those who received it later on a grammatical measure, with distributions that overlap substantially. A journalist writes that the research proves language cannot be acquired after age three. What two specific reporting errors does the sentence make?
questions.answer: It converts an average group difference with overlapping distributions into a categorical rule for every individual, and it identifies a critical period where the data support a graded sensitive period.
questions.distractor: It fails to report the sample size and the exact age at which the group difference reached significance, which are the two omissions that would make the claim defensible.
questions.correction: Sample size and the significance threshold are technical details; the sentence's errors are interpretive and much larger. First, an average difference with wide overlap between groups supports a probabilistic statement about the populations, not a rule that applies to an individual learner, and the overlap is itself information: many later learners outperform many earlier learners. Second, the finding is about a gradient in outcome against age of first language access, which is the weaker sensitive-period claim, whereas the word proves asserts a closed window. A third issue worth naming is measurement: grammatical measures often have bounded ranges, and bounded measures compress high performers, which can make the age effect look sharper than it is. Compare the 'What We Did Not Claim' section of the American Sign Language review in lesson 63.

questions.prompt: A developmental imaging paper reports that a reward-reactivity index correlates with a risk-taking measure at r = 0.20 in 34 adolescents, and that an imbalance score computed as reward minus control shows a significant age trend. A reviewer objects that the imbalance score is unreliable. What does that objection predict about the reported correlations, and what should the authors have done?
questions.answer: Unreliable difference scores attenuate correlations, so the observed correlation is expected to be smaller than the true association, and the authors should have reported the reliability of each component and of the difference score alongside the correlation.
questions.distractor: Unreliable difference scores inflate correlations by adding variance to the predictor, so the authors should have reported a corrected coefficient that removes the unreliable component.
questions.correction: Measurement error in a predictor attenuates the observed association toward zero rather than inflating it, which is the opposite of the distractor's claim. A difference score inherits the error of both components and its reliability is typically lower than either one, so an observed r of 0.20 may correspond to a larger true association, or the construct may simply not be measurable with adequate precision in that sample. Either way the reporting requirement is the same: state the reliability of each component and of the composite, so readers can judge whether the study was capable of detecting the association it tested. The sample of 34 participants also limits precision, since detecting a correlation near 0.20 requires roughly two hundred participants at conventional power. See lesson 64 and the statistical-evaluation review on dual-systems models.

questions.prompt: A clinic advertises a brief memory screen with 90 per cent sensitivity and 90 per cent specificity, and states that a positive result means early impairment. In a general population where the condition being screened for has a prevalence of about 1 per cent, what does the arithmetic from this unit imply about the statement?
questions.answer: At a 1 per cent prevalence, about 9 of 108 positive results belong to people who have the condition, roughly 8 per cent, so a positive result cannot be described as meaning impairment.
questions.distractor: At a 1 per cent prevalence the test is more accurate than in a clinic, because there are more healthy people against whom its specificity can be demonstrated.
questions.correction: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and stay fixed here, but predictive value depends on prevalence, and lower prevalence means most positives are false positives. Work it in a thousand people: 10 have the condition and 9 test positive; 990 do not and 99 test positive; 9 divided by 108 is about 8 per cent. Raise the prevalence to 20 per cent, as in a specialist service, and the same test yields 180 true positives and 80 false positives, about 69 per cent. The distractor is a non-sequitur: a larger healthy group increases the absolute number of false positives without improving how well the test detects the condition. A screen changes the probability that further assessment is warranted; it does not classify a person, which is the central point of lesson 65.

units.title: Mechanisms and interventions put to the test

lessons.title: Memory reconsolidation: the biology, the boundary conditions, and why the debate is unresolved
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to state the reconsolidation hypothesis precisely, describe the two experiments that would distinguish it from its main rivals, and explain why several well-designed studies have failed to find the effect in humans. Start with the terms. Consolidation is the set of processes by which a newly formed memory becomes stable over time, and it is sensitive to interference and to protein synthesis blockade around the time of learning. Retrieval is the act of reactivating a memory. Destabilisation is the hypothesised return of a consolidated memory to a labile state after retrieval. Reconsolidation is the re-stabilisation that follows, again requiring protein synthesis. The primary animal demonstration is the study published in Nature in 2000 by Nader, Schafe and LeDoux, which reported that fear memories in rats required protein synthesis in the amygdala in order to persist after retrieval - that is, blockade given after reactivation, not after learning, impaired later retention. Note the era and the model: 2000, rodents, auditory fear conditioning, with a protein synthesis inhibitor. The hypothesis has since been applied to humans, most prominently with the beta-adrenergic blocker propranolol as a research tool, which is administered experimentally to test whether a retrieved fear memory can be weakened. The review 'An update on memory reconsolidation updating', by Lee, Nader and Schiller, is unusually candid about the state of play. It reports that retrieval in itself is insufficient to trigger destabilisation of a fear memory, as assessed by the impact of propranolol, and that an error in prediction about what happens during reactivation appears to be required. It devotes a box to alternative interpretations of retrieval-dependent amnesia, a section to the theoretical challenges of reactivation-dependent lability, and a section titled 'The reliability of reconsolidation effects'. The failures matter as much as the successes. One study, 'In Search for Boundary Conditions of Reconsolidation', reports a failure of the predicted fear-memory interference, with the propranolol manipulation itself checked, and another preregistered study, 'Demarcating the boundary conditions of memory reconsolidation: An unsuccessful replication', used Bayesian sequential updating and reported no evidence for an effect of propranolol on disrupting reconsolidation, adding that it also found no evidence for complete fear extinction in any group. Three qualifications frame the honest summary. First, negative results do not erase the animal findings; they constrain their translation, which is the correct scientific outcome of a boundary-condition search that is going badly. Second, the standard human readout is behaviour - startle potentiation, expectancy ratings - and behaviour cannot distinguish an erased trace from a trace that is intact but not expressed. Third, this literature is explicitly contested, so it should be taught with the disagreement visible rather than resolved in the telling. Nothing here is clinical guidance; the studies discussed are experimental paradigms, not treatments.
lessons.example: Two calculations show how a contested literature should be read. First, translate an illustrative effect into percentages so the contrast can be compared across studies rather than across adjectives. Suppose a fear-conditioning study reports startle potentiation of 60 units in a control condition, 30 units in a group given a blocking drug shortly after retrieval, and 58 units in a group given the same drug several hours after retrieval. The early group shows a reduction of (60 minus 30) divided by 60, which is 50 per cent; the late group shows (60 minus 58) divided by 60, which is 3.3 per cent. If the timing contrast is real, it supports a narrow post-retrieval window; if the same comparison fails in a preregistered replication with more participants, that is information about reliability, not proof that the first study was fraudulent. Note that these numbers are constructed for arithmetic practice; they are not taken from any study and must not be cited as findings. Second, quantify the multiple-comparison problem in boundary-condition research. A boundary condition is a variable that determines whether the effect appears: memory age, memory strength, the number of reminder cues, the interval between retrieval and drug, individual differences. If a team tests ten such moderators separately at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, the chance of at least one false positive is one minus 0.95 to the tenth power, which is 0.401 - about 40 per cent. Report the count of tests, pre-specify the primary one, and treat the rest as exploratory, or the literature will fill with apparent boundary conditions that are sampling noise. Combine the two calculations when you read a claim: an effect size expressed as a percentage reduction, and the number of chances the analyst had to find it.
lessons.question: A well-powered preregistered study reports no effect of a post-retrieval drug on fear memory, while an earlier study with thirty participants per group reported a large effect. Which conclusion is best supported?
lessons.answer: The effect is not robust across designs and conditions, so the appropriate conclusion is that the phenomenon is conditional and less reliably translatable than the earlier report suggested, not that the underlying animal biology has been refuted or that the newer study is necessarily correct.
lessons.distractor: The preregistered study supersedes the earlier one, so the reconsolidation hypothesis should be considered falsified in humans.
lessons.correction: Preregistration and better power make the newer study a stronger test of the specific hypothesis it registered, but a single null result does not falsify a hypothesis with positive animal evidence and multiple positive human studies, and it cannot rule out the boundary conditions the design did not manipulate. The correct summary keeps the disagreement visible: some conditions produce the effect, replication has been unreliable, the theoretical mechanism - destabilisation requiring prediction error, then restabilisation - remains the leading account, and alternative explanations of retrieval-dependent amnesia have not been excluded. That is the posture the review by Lee, Nader and Schiller takes when it separates the reliability of the effects from the mechanism. The distractor's error is treating one design as decisive; the mirror error is treating the original positive result as decisive. Both fail the standard this lesson is teaching.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: a memory trace, or engram, is the physical change that carries a memory, which cannot currently be observed directly at the systems level in humans; retrieval is the process of reactivating it; reactivation here means presenting a reminder cue that brings the memory back. Protein synthesis blockade means administering an agent that interferes with the production of new proteins, used in animals and, in human work, drugs that act on particular signalling pathways. Propranolol is a beta-adrenergic receptor blocker used experimentally in this literature because noradrenergic signalling is implicated in emotional memory; this course describes it as a research tool and offers no clinical guidance about any medication. Boundary condition means a factor that determines whether an effect occurs. Comprehension of a memory, that is, whether its content can be reported, is a separate question from its expression in a physiological response, which is why expectancy ratings and startle measures can dissociate. Extinction is new learning that suppresses the expression of an old memory rather than removing it.
depth.mechanism: The hypothesised mechanism has four steps. A consolidated memory is retrieved by a reminder; the retrieval process generates a prediction error - the reminder predicts something that does not occur, or occurs differently - and this surprise is what makes the trace labile; the labile trace must then be restabilised, a process requiring new protein synthesis and, in emotional memory, adrenergic signalling; if restabilisation is disrupted, later expression is reduced. This account predicts a narrow window: the disruptor must be given close to retrieval, and retrieval must involve a mismatch. Both predictions have been used as tests, and both have produced mixed results, which is why the field's own review labels the reliability of the effects as a separate question from their theoretical coherence. Three rival explanations must be excluded before accepting the mechanism. First, retrieval-dependent amnesia could reflect impaired retrieval rather than impaired storage, in which case the memory may still exist and could be recovered by another cue. Second, the drug or manipulation could act on performance or on the state of the animal or participant rather than on the trace. Third, the observed reduction could be enhanced extinction or increased interference rather than destabilisation and failed restabilisation. Each rival makes a distinctive prediction - for example, recovery with a different reminder cue favours the retrieval-failure account - and much of the argument in the literature is about whether those tests were run and passed.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the fear-conditioning paradigm with an everyday claim you may encounter: that a technique allows you to rewrite a troubling memory. The laboratory paradigm has three properties that the marketing version usually lacks. It studies a simple conditioned response with a precisely timed learning episode, a controlled reminder, and a physiological readout; the memory content is trivial by design. It manipulates a pharmacological or procedural variable with a known action and measures the effect against a control condition in the same session. And its results, as this lesson documents, have been hard to replicate in preregistered human studies. The claim about rewriting memories, by contrast, usually involves memories that are old, strong, emotionally significant, personally meaningful and embedded in a life - exactly the boundary conditions the literature identifies as least favourable for destabilisation, according to the same review's discussion of strong and old memories. It also typically provides no controlled reminder, no way to verify that the original memory changed rather than the person's narrative about it, and no objective outcome. The contrast teaches the general rule: when a mechanism is contested in a controlled setting, claims about it in an uncontrolled setting require a higher burden of evidence, not a lower one.
depth.mistake: The most common error is overgeneralising from mechanism to control: 'reconsolidation shows that memories can be erased, so any memory can be removed if you reactivate it'. Every clause fails. Destabilisation has been difficult to reproduce reliably in humans; prediction error, not mere reactivation, appears necessary; memory age and strength are boundary conditions; and the observed effect in successful studies is a reduction in a physiological response, not the removal of a memory. A second error is treating a debate as settled because a review exists: a review can be a vehicle for advocacy, and the same literature contains its own section on reliability. A third is the mirror of the second - dismissing the mechanism because of one failed replication and thereby ignoring substantial positive animal evidence. The diagnostic question for any contested claim in this unit will be the same: what would distinguish the hypothesis from its rivals, and has that test been run and repeated?
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Write a 150-word preregistration summary for a human reconsolidation study that would genuinely inform the debate. State the memory paradigm, the reactivation manipulation and how you will verify that prediction error occurred, the disruption variable, the two measurement occasions, the primary outcome with its units, the primary statistical test, and one rival explanation with the analysis that would separate it. Model response: 'Paradigm: differential fear conditioning with a coloured-shape cue and a mild aversive sound. Reactivation: a single reminder with an explicitly signalled mismatch, verified by expectancy ratings within the session. Disruption: experimental blocking agent versus matched placebo, double-blind. Outcome: startle potentiation difference scores at reactivation and at 24 hours, in microvolts, pre-specified as the primary measure. Test: between-group comparison of change scores, with the confidence interval and an equivalence test reported. Rival: enhanced extinction, tested by including a no-reactivation control that receives the same extinction procedure, so any group difference cannot be attributed to extinction alone.' Self-review rubric: two points for a verified reactivation manipulation; two for a pre-specified primary outcome with units; two for the rival-explanation control; one for stating the equivalence or precision expectation rather than only a significance test.
depth.summary: Reconsolidation is a four-step hypothesis - retrieval, prediction-error-driven destabilisation, protein-synthesis-dependent restabilisation, reduced later expression - supported by animal work from 2000 onwards and contested in humans, where preregistered studies have failed to find the effect and where the standard readouts cannot distinguish storage from expression. Reading it well requires three habits: express effects as comparable quantities, count the number of chances the analysts had to find a boundary condition, and keep rivals on the table with the tests that would separate them. The same habits apply to any contested mechanism claim you meet later in the course. Lesson 67 moves from memory to attention, where the contested claim is not a mechanism but the practical one that people can do several demanding things at once.

visual.title: The four-step hypothesis and the tests that would break it
visual.description: A horizontal timeline for the hypothesised mechanism with a row of predicted interventions beneath it and a row of rival explanations with their distinguishing tests below that.
steps: Step 1 RETRIEVAL: a reminder cue reactivates the consolidated trace; label reads WITHOUT PREDICTION ERROR, NO DESTABILISATION.
Step 2 DESTABILISATION: the trace becomes labile; side note marks the narrow window measured in hours.
Step 3 RESTABILISATION: new protein synthesis and adrenergic signalling required; a blocking agent given at this point is predicted to reduce later expression.
Step 4 LATER EXPRESSION: the readout, usually a physiological response; label reads REDUCED EXPRESSION IS NOT PROOF THAT STORAGE CHANGED.

Rival row: R1 IMPAIRED RETRIEVAL - test with an alternative reminder cue and check for recovery; R2 PERFORMANCE OR STATE EFFECT - test with a matched placebo and a drug-only control without reactivation; R3 ENHANCED EXTINCTION - test with a no-reactivation control that receives identical extinction.

Evidence row across the bottom: 2000 animal demonstration (rats, protein synthesis blockade); non-replication in preregistered human studies; review conclusion that reliability and mechanism are separate questions.
Labelling note: constructed numbers must never be entered on this diagram; each row is labelled DESIGN LOGIC, not a data table.

lessons.title: Attention as selection, and what the evidence about media multitasking actually shows
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to define attention as a selection process rather than a resource, describe the load manipulation and its main criticism, and state the current status of the media-multitasking finding after replication attempts and meta-analysis. Attention in this course means the set of processes that bias which information is processed, and how deeply, given that the system cannot process everything equally. Two consequences follow immediately. Selection can be driven by the stimulus, as when a sudden movement captures processing, or by the task, as when you search for a friend in a crowd. And selection has a cost: what is not selected is processed less, which is why the phenomenon is studied through interference, capture and search rather than through a feeling of focus. The load account proposes that the amount of perceptual processing a task demands determines whether task-irrelevant stimuli are processed: under high perceptual load, distractors have little effect, while under low load they intrude. The review 'Attentional Load and Attentional Boost' works through this evidence and then complicates it, because detecting a target for one task broadly enhances perceptual processing of stimuli that appear at the same time - the attentional boost effect - which a simple capacity story does not predict. Its later sections on temporal selection and on reconciling the boost with load, and its section on the dual-task interaction model, are the constructive part of the argument. The critique 'Conceptual and methodological concerns in the theory of perceptual load' attacks the framework's foundations: circularity, because whether a condition counts as high load can be defined by whether distractors were processed; dilution rather than load as an alternative explanation for some results; and vagueness in distinguishing perceptual, cognitive and sensory load. Read the two together and you have a live methodological dispute about a widely taught theory. Now media multitasking. The 2009 study by Ophir, Nass and Wagner, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that people scoring high on a media-use questionnaire performed worse on measures of distraction filtering. The finding became a staple of commentary; a PNAS commentary interpreted it as evidence that heavy media multitaskers run breadth-biased cognitive control, treating more information as equally worth attending. Then came replication. The 2017 paper 'Cognitive control in media multitaskers: Two replication studies and a meta-Analysis' reports that its meta-analysis of 39 effect sizes yielded a weak but significant association between media multitasking and distractibility that turned nonsignificant after correction for small-study effects. That is the state of the evidence: a small association whose significance depends on how publication bias and small studies are handled. Three qualifications. First, media multitasking is measured by self-report questionnaires, so the predictor is a belief about one's own behaviour and is subject to recall and social-desirability effects. Second, the direction of causation is unresolved: heavy media use may reduce attentional control, or people with more distractible attention may prefer it. Third, the neuroscience of selection itself supplies a useful constraint: the classic clinical case of contralateral neglect, described in Neuroscience Online Section 4, Chapter 9, sub-section 9.2, shows that damage can abolish attention to an entire half of space, which demonstrates that selection is spatially organised and has a neural basis without showing that attention is one thing located anywhere.
lessons.example: Two calculations decide how much weight the media-multitasking literature can bear. First, power. Detecting a correlation of 0.10 with 80 per cent power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 requires roughly 783 participants; a correlation of 0.20 requires roughly 194; a correlation of 0.30 requires about 85. Now note that the published studies in this literature typically have samples in the dozens. A small study is unlikely to detect a true small association, so the ones that do report it are disproportionately those that happened to overestimate it - the winner's curse - which is exactly the mechanism that produces a weak meta-analytic estimate that survives only until small-study correction is applied. Second, the substantive size. A correlation of 0.20 explains 4 per cent of the variance in the outcome, and a corrected estimate below 0.10 explains under 1 per cent. Those numbers do not make the effect unreal, but they bound the meaning: a self-reported media habit is not a powerful explanation of individual differences in distractibility, and a headline claiming that multitasking is destroying your ability to focus is making a much larger claim than 4 per cent of variance supports. Now add a third quantity that is often confused with the others: switching overhead. If a person interleaves two twenty-minute tasks with four switches, and each switch costs an assumed half-minute of reorientation, the total time is 40 plus 2 minutes, an overhead of 5 per cent. That is an illustration of an arithmetic structure, not a measured finding, and it belongs to task switching, a different phenomenon from media multitasking and from dual-task interference. Keeping the three apart - self-reported habit, concurrent dual-task interference, and sequential switching cost - is most of the discipline this lesson teaches.
lessons.question: A reviewer objects that an experiment claiming to show 'high perceptual load blocks distractors' manipulated load by making the display harder until distractors stopped interfering. Why is that objection serious?
lessons.answer: Because load is then identified by the outcome it is supposed to explain, so the claim becomes circular: the condition is high load precisely because the distractors did not interfere, and no independent prediction about what high load will do remains.
lessons.distractor: Because making the display harder also increases cognitive and sensory demands, so the experiment cannot isolate perceptual load from other kinds of load.
lessons.correction: The second objection is a real but secondary problem, discussed in the same critique as the vagueness of the load categories. The primary problem is circularity, which undermines the theory's predictive power rather than its measurement. If load is defined operationally by failure of distraction, then the statement that high load reduces distraction is a tautology, and the framework cannot generate a risky prediction such as 'this specific manipulation, defined by a stimulus property independent of performance, will reduce distractor processing by a measurable amount'. The remedy is to define load before measuring interference - by the number of relevant items searched, for example, with the behavioural check reported separately - and to pre-specify the outcome. This is the same discipline you applied to the dual-systems imbalance score in lesson 64 and to boundary conditions in lesson 66: a construct defined by its own outcome cannot be tested.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: selection is the prioritisation of some information over other information; capture is the involuntary prioritisation of a salient or suddenly appearing stimulus; interference is the reduction in performance caused by processing something else; a distractor is a stimulus that competes with the target; perceptual load refers to the amount of relevant perceptual processing required by a task, as distinct from cognitive load such as holding items in mind; dilution refers to the possibility that adding more items, whether relevant or not, weakens the influence of any single item; dual-task interference is the mutual cost of two tasks performed concurrently; a switching cost is the decrement in performance when attention moves between tasks sequentially; media multitasking questionnaires ask people to report how often they use more than one medium at once. Two cautions: 'multitasking' in popular usage mixes concurrent and sequential cases, and 'attention' as a psychological construct is not identical to arousal, alertness or effort.
depth.mechanism: Why would selection have a cost at all? A selective process must resolve competition among representations that are simultaneously active. Competition can be resolved by biasing the representations relevant to the current task and suppressing the others, and it can be resolved by limiting the depth of processing of unattended material. These two routes make different predictions. Bias accounts predict measurable enhancement of attended and suppression of ignored features even when stimulus displays are identical; gating accounts predict that unattended items are registered but not consolidated into reportable representations. The attentional boost effect constrains both: detecting a target for one task enhanced memory and perceptual processing of unrelated stimuli presented at the same moment, which looks like a transient enhancement rather than global capacity depletion, and it forced models to include the temporal structure of task events rather than only instantaneous load. The media-multitasking literature, by contrast, is not a mechanism study at all. It measures a self-reported habit and an attentional outcome and correlates them, leaving causal direction unaddressed, and the correlation itself is small once small-study effects are corrected. Structurally, this literature has the same design weakness as the expertise comparisons in lesson 62: the experience was not assigned, so preference and ability are confounded with the habit.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the laboratory load paradigm with a real-world claim about studying, and watch which evidence is relevant. The claim is that students who keep a messaging application open while reading learn less from the same text. The laboratory version of this question is a dual-task interference study: reading comprehension measured with and without a secondary task, with materials and difficulty matched, and with a check that participants actually performed the secondary task. That design can establish that concurrent demands reduce comprehension on those materials for those participants. The real-world claim needs more: measurement of what the student actually did rather than what they report, a comparison that holds time-on-task constant, and an outcome that reflects learning after a delay rather than immediate comprehension. Two further distinctions sharpen the analysis. Keeping an application open is not the same as responding to a message: the mere presence of a possible interruption, in some studies, can affect performance on demanding tasks, whereas the interruption itself has a different time signature. And the cost of interruption depends on where it lands: interrupting a low-demand task costs less than interrupting a demanding one, which is the practical version of the load argument and does not require the theory to be fully settled. Use the distinctions, not the slogan.
depth.mistake: The first error is treating attention as a muscle that multitasking exercises, which confuses practice at switching with improved concurrent capacity, and which the evidence does not support in either direction. The second is the opposite hyperbole, that humans cannot multitask at all. Skilled performance does include well-practised combinations, especially when one task is overlearned or automatic and when the tasks use different modalities, and dismissing this class of cases makes the sceptical position easy to refute. The third error is importing a number you cannot source: the widely quoted claim that interruptions impose a fixed percentage of lost time usually traces back to a specific industrial study with specific materials, and the figure should not be attached to whichever task you happen to be discussing. The diagnostic habit is to ask three questions: was the predictor self-reported or measured; was the outcome measured concurrently or after a delay; and is the quantity a correlation, an interference cost or a switching cost? Most bad claims fail at least one of these.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Design a 10-minute self-experiment on your own reading, then audit the design. Conditions: read two comparable passages, one with a messaging application open and one without, counterbalanced across two days in the opposite order. Measure comprehension with three questions per passage, and record how many interruptions actually occurred rather than how many you expected. Then answer four audit questions: (1) is the predictor measured or self-reported; (2) is the outcome immediate or delayed; (3) which of the three quantities - correlation, interference cost, switching cost - does your comparison estimate; (4) what single alternative explanation is most likely, given that passages differ and your level of fatigue varies across days. Model response: 'Predictor: measured count of interruptions. Outcome: immediate, three questions, small and unreliable. Quantity: interference cost on that task in that session. Main alternative: passage difficulty and time of day. Conclusion: I can say something about my own reading under interruption today, not about multitasking in general.' Self-review rubric: two points for measuring interruptions rather than assuming them; two for naming the quantity being estimated; two for naming a specific alternative explanation; two for restricting the conclusion to the conditions actually tested.
depth.summary: Attention is selection with a cost, studied through interference and capture; the load framework is a leading account of when distractors are processed, and it has a documented circularity problem that you should check for in any study you read. The attentional boost effect shows the story is more than instantaneous capacity. Media multitasking rests mainly on self-report questionnaires, and after two replication studies and a meta-analysis of 39 effect sizes the association with distractibility is weak and loses significance once small-study effects are corrected, in a literature whose typical samples are far too small to estimate an effect that size. Keep correlation, dual-task interference and switching cost apart, and the practical claims become tractable. Lesson 68 moves to a control distinction whose behavioural signature can be measured directly: habit versus intention.

lessons.title: Habit and intention: two control systems, how they interact, and what 'habit' does not mean
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to define goal-directed and habitual control by the tests that distinguish them, describe how the two interact during learning and in everyday settings, and correct three popular misstatements about habits. The distinction is operational. Goal-directed control selects an action because of its current consequences: change the value of the outcome, or degrade the relationship between the action and the outcome, and the action changes. Habitual control selects an action because of a cue and its past pairing with a reward: change the outcome value and the action persists. Two laboratory tests implement these definitions. In an outcome devaluation test, participants learn action-outcome relationships, then one outcome is devalued - for example by feeding the participant to satiety on that specific food - and the question is whether responding for that outcome falls. In contingency degradation, the outcome is made available regardless of the response, and the question is whether responding declines. A third paradigm, the slips-of-action task, presents cues that signal outcomes in a phase where the outcomes are no longer delivered and asks participants to withhold the previously rewarded response, which measures the failure to use current knowledge to suppress a cue-driven response. Neuroscience Online, Section 3, Chapter 4, describes the neural side in sub-section 4.6, 'Functions of the Basal Ganglia', and 4.8, 'Habit learning in striatum', with 4.9 describing patients with basal ganglia disorders who are impaired at learning new tasks while performing previously learned movements. Read that material as evidence for a contribution, not for a single seat of habit: the loops described include cortex and thalamus, and the chapters on motor cortex and cerebellum in the same section describe other contributions. A recent review, 'Habit and persistence', complicates the standard story constructively. Its section 'Are habits unusually sticky and persistent?' examines resistance to extinction, resistance to contingency degradation, vulnerability to relapse, and resistance to context change, and it concludes that habit should not be equated with unusual persistence: the function of habit learning may be to make behaviour automatic and efficient in a particular context rather than to make it strong. Its final section treats habit conversion as a behavioural end point. An experiment-and-diary study of the balance between the two systems, 'Investigating the balance between goal-directed and habitual control in experimental and real-life settings', reports that a stable cue and context for the target behaviour is needed and that the time before a habit reaches its maximal self-reported strength can vary widely - a caution against the popular claim that a behaviour becomes automatic after a fixed number of days. Three qualifications follow. First, the tests measure sensitivity to value and contingency, so an action can be cue-driven yet still under some current-goal influence; the systems are better treated as competing influences than as two exclusive modes. Second, most evidence comes from laboratory tasks with small rewards, and the transfer to complex everyday behaviour is an inference. Third, self-reported habit strength is a report about experienced automaticity, not a direct measure of the underlying control process.
lessons.example: Work through the arithmetic of the devaluation test, then the arithmetic of the everyday claim. In a slips-of-action task, participants learn that particular stimuli are associated with particular outcomes, then learn that one outcome is no longer available, and then see the stimuli again with instructions to respond only if the outcome is still valuable. Suppose the habitual-response rate - pressing for the devalued outcome - is 60 per cent in one group and 50 per cent in another, where 50 per cent is chance. To detect a difference between two proportions of 60 and 50 per cent with 80 per cent power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, you need roughly 388 participants per group. Studies with 20 or 30 participants per group can produce a difference this size only by chance a large fraction of the time, which is why single small results in this area should be read as suggestive. The same arithmetic applies to any comparison of proportions, including adherence data. Now the everyday calculator. A widely repeated claim says that a behaviour becomes automatic after a fixed period, often quoted in weeks. Reputable summaries of the habit-formation literature do not support a fixed number: the study in this lesson's readings says the time before a habit reaches its maximal self-reported strength can vary widely, and it emphasises that a stable cue and context and relatively frequent performance are what the models need. Convert the frequency condition into arithmetic instead of a promise: performing a behaviour on 80 per cent of 30 days is 24 days of practice, and on 70 per cent of 90 days is 63 days, while a plan that depends on a decision every day costs whatever rehearsal it takes - five minutes daily for a month is 150 minutes, or 2.5 hours, spent deciding rather than doing. That last figure is the useful part of the habit literature for practical purposes: a cue-based plan replaces repeated deliberation, which is why implementation intentions - pre-specified if-then plans that bind an action to a situation - are studied as a way of transferring control to the environment.
lessons.question: A student reports that she keeps snacking in the evening 'out of habit' but that she can stop when she has just eaten a large dinner. Which statement about the underlying control is best supported?
lessons.answer: Her snacking is still sensitive to the current value of the outcome, which is the defining feature of goal-directed control, so the label 'habit' is doing useful describing work but not the explanatory work the word usually implies.
lessons.distractor: Because she snacks in the evening on most days, the behaviour has become habitual, and the fact that a large dinner temporarily suppresses it is consistent with habit being a strong but masked automatic response.
lessons.correction: Frequency alone does not establish habitual control. The defining test is sensitivity to outcome value and to the action-outcome contingency, and the student's own description indicates sensitivity: she reduces the behaviour when the outcome is worth less. That is goal-directed control. The distractor's version cannot be falsified, because any failure to observe insensitivity is explained away as masking, which is what makes 'strong but masked' a rhetorical move rather than a scientific one. The lesson's other half matters here too: prompt her to look for the cue structure instead. If the snacking occurs in a specific context at a specific time and is predicted, the productive question is which cue can be re-linked to a different action, and an if-then plan changes that cue-behaviour mapping without requiring the person to re-decide each evening.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: an outcome is the consequence that makes an action worth performing; devaluation reduces the current value of an outcome without changing the action-outcome pairing; contingency degradation weakens the relationship between the response and the outcome while leaving the outcome available; a discriminative stimulus is a cue that indicates a particular response will be reinforced; automaticity in this literature means the response is initiated with little deliberation by a cue, not that it cannot be modified; habit strength in questionnaire research means the person's self-reported experience of doing the behaviour without thinking; implementation intentions are pre-specified plans of the form 'when situation X arises, I will perform response Y'; a slips-of-action task measures whether an instructed, currently relevant goal can suppress a previously learned cue-response association. Keep habit distinct from compulsion, which involves repeated behaviour despite adverse consequences and is a clinical concept outside this course's scope.
depth.mechanism: How do cue-driven responses come to dominate? A cue paired repeatedly with a rewarded response acquires the ability to trigger that response; as training continues, the response becomes less dependent on moment-to-moment evaluation of the outcome, which is the shift the devaluation test detects. The textbook's basal ganglia sections supply the circuit description: information from cortical areas projects through the basal ganglia and back to cortex in a loop, and the striatum is described as supporting the learning of actions tied to their outcomes, so an intact loop is needed to learn which actions pay. Two corrections keep the mechanism honest. First, the shift is a matter of degree and of context, not a switch that moves a behaviour between stores. Second, the review 'Habit and persistence' argues that habit should not be defined by persistence: habits of the laboratory kind are not uniformly harder to extinguish, to degrade, or to change with context than goal-directed actions, so mechanism claims that treat habit as the sticky state have to be supported rather than assumed. Relapse and context sensitivity are where the interesting questions live, and they are also where the everyday case differs most from the laboratory: real contexts contain many cues, distractors and competing goals, and a laboratory task with one cue and one reward removes most of that structure.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a laboratory habit with a behaviour often labelled habitual in an organisational setting: a clinician who always walks a fixed route through a ward, or a driver who takes the same road home. Apply the tests rather than the label. Would the route change if its outcome were devalued - for example, if the corridor were closed or the destination moved? If the person takes a different route the moment it becomes slower, the behaviour is under goal-directed control with an efficient, well-learned routine underneath, which is not the same as insensitivity to the outcome. Would it persist if it became useless? A route that stops serving its purpose but continues to be taken is closer to the habitual pattern. Now consider the practical consequence of confusing these cases. If a behaviour is well-learned but goal-sensitive, then changing outcomes and information changes it quickly, and interventions should focus on making the better option easy and known. If the same behaviour is cue-driven and outcome-insensitive, then changing outcomes will underperform and the effective lever is likely to be the cue or the environment. The distinction is thus a diagnostic tool with practical consequences, not a taxonomy for its own sake. The same reasoning underlies the outcome-devaluation and contingency-degradation procedures in the review you are reading.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first is converting the popular day-count claim into a rule; the literature varies with behaviour complexity, cue stability and frequency, and the reading in this lesson states explicitly that the time to maximal self-reported strength can vary widely. The second is treating habit as a synonym for any repeated behaviour, which loses the diagnostic power of the outcome-sensitivity test and makes behavioural interventions unfocused. The third is the corollary that habits are uniquely persistent and therefore the right target for every behaviour-change effort; the review in this lesson's readings examines resistance to extinction, contingency degradation, relapse and context change, and shows that the case for special stickiness is weaker than the popular account assumes. Diagnostic question: if the outcome stopped mattering right now, what would the person actually do, and what is the evidence? If nobody has asked that, the word habit has been used as a description, not an explanation.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Choose one recurring behaviour of your own and analyse it in at most 200 words. State the cue (time, place, preceding action, or emotional state); state the outcome that currently maintains it; state what would count as evidence of outcome insensitivity (what you would still do if the outcome stopped mattering); then draft one if-then plan for the situation you identified and one competing plan that changes the outcome instead of the cue. Model response: 'Cue: sitting down at the desk after dinner. Outcome: relief from a task I am avoiding. Evidence of insensitivity would be continuing to open the same application even when the task it serves has already been completed for the day, which does not describe me, so the control is probably goal-directed and the cue is incidental. Plan A, cue-based: if I sit down after dinner, then I open the assignment file first. Plan B, outcome-based: if I notice avoidance relief is the point, then I schedule the avoided task for a fixed earlier slot and remove the task from the evening.' Self-review rubric: two points for a specific cue rather than a broad category; two for stating what evidence of insensitivity would look like; two for writing both a cue-based and an outcome-based plan; one for saying which plan the evidence favours and why.
depth.summary: Goal-directed and habitual control are distinguished by sensitivity to outcome value and to the action-outcome contingency, not by how often a behaviour is repeated. The circuit contribution of cortico-basal ganglia loops to learning action-outcome and cue-response associations is well described, while the claim that habits are uniquely persistent is weaker than its popularity suggests. The time to maximal automaticity varies widely rather than following a fixed schedule, the cue structure and its frequency are what the habit-formation literature emphasises, and the two systems are best treated as competing influences that a single behaviour can mix. That framework - identify the measurement, define the construct by a test, and separate mechanism from practical advice - is what lesson 69 applies to interventions, where pharmacological and behavioural trials can establish different things.

lessons.title: Pharmacological and behavioural interventions: what each kind of trial can and cannot show
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a drug trial and a behavioural trial each establish in principle, identify the design feature that carries the burden of inference in each, and explain why the two cannot be evaluated with one checklist. This lesson is about study design and evidence, not about treatment; it contains no advice about any medication or therapy for any person, and clinical decisions belong with qualified professionals. Begin with the structural difference. A drug trial can usually blind participants and investigators: the comparison condition can be an identical-looking inactive substance, so that expectations, contact with staff, and the ritual of taking something are matched between arms, and the pharmacological effect is isolated by subtraction. That is the strength of the pharmacological design, and it is also its limit: the trial estimates the effect of the drug under those blinded conditions, in those participants, on those outcome measures and over that follow-up. A behavioural trial cannot easily be blinded: participants know whether they are practising something, and sham versions of a training task can differ in engagement, enjoyment and effort, which are exactly the mechanisms that could produce improvement. The behavioural design therefore carries its inference on a different feature: the active control, chosen so that expectancy and contact are comparable, with measured participants' expectations. The systematic review of placebo-control methodology for computerised cognitive training sets out this taxonomy in its own section headings, distinguishing active controls of the active-ingredient type from similar-form types, and passive controls of the no-contact and passive-task types, and it devotes sections to why controlling for a placebo effect is imperative and to the difference between a placebo effect and a motivation effect. The reason this is not a technicality is demonstrated by a placebo study in cognitive training published in 2016, in which the same training procedure was administered to two groups recruited with different flyers: the group recruited in a way that implied the training would raise intelligence reported substantially higher belief that intelligence is malleable (the authors report a large between-group difference on that belief index, with a standardised value above two), completed the same amount of training, and showed post-training fluid-intelligence gains. The authors concluded that their positive effects on fluid intelligence were the result of the recruitment framing, and they converted the size into interpretable units: about 0.5 standard deviations, roughly 6 to 8 IQ points on the scale they used. Expectancy alone produced a gain of the magnitude that many training studies report as a training effect. Now add the outcome-measure problem, which affects both designs. A framework paper on surrogate endpoints defines the issue: many trials measure intermediate quantities such as a biomarker or a test score rather than how patients feel, function or survive, and interpreting an intermediate outcome as if it stood in for the clinical outcome requires argument, not assumption. A meta-analysis of computerised cognitive training in mild cognitive impairment illustrates the scale of the effects at stake: across the included studies, global cognitive function improved by a standardised mean difference of 0.23 with a confidence interval from 0.03 to 0.44, a small effect on a cognitive test, on a surrogate measure. Three qualifications. First, small average effects on surrogates can still matter, but their interpretation requires evidence about function, not about the surrogate alone. Second, the two designs have different failure modes: drug trials can be underpowered for the effect they seek, and behavioural trials can be unblinded and expectancy-confounded. Third, neither design, however clean, establishes what should be done; that is a separate question involving effects, harms, costs and preferences.
lessons.example: Compute the power arithmetic that governs how much either kind of trial can settle. For a two-group comparison with equal groups at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, detecting a standardised effect of 0.2 with 80 per cent power requires roughly 393 participants per group; detecting 0.1 requires roughly 1,570 per group; detecting 0.5 requires 63. Now reverse the calculation for a study you might actually encounter: a trial with 40 participants per group has about 14 per cent power to detect an effect of 0.2 standard deviations. Fourteen per cent power means that if the true effect were 0.2, the study would fail to reach significance about 86 per cent of the time, so a null result from it carries almost no information, and a positive result from it is very likely to be an overestimate. This is the arithmetic behind the repeated pattern in this unit: small studies produce large, unstable effects, and independent replication shrinks them. Combine it with the expectancy result from the 2016 placebo study, in which a framing manipulation alone was associated with about 0.5 standard deviations of fluid-intelligence change, equivalent to roughly 6 to 8 points on the IQ scale used. Put the two numbers side by side: a plausible expectancy effect of 0.5 standard deviations is larger than the 0.2 standard deviation effect that requires nearly 800 participants to detect across two arms. A behavioural trial without an active control and without measured expectations is therefore not merely imprecise; it is systematically biased in the direction of its own hypothesis, and the bias can exceed the effect being sought. For a drug trial the same arithmetic applies to power, but the expectancy term is partly removed by successful blinding - which is why the interpretation of a drug effect depends on reported blinding integrity, allocation concealment, and whether the outcome is a surrogate or a clinical measure.
lessons.question: A randomised double-blind trial reports that a compound improved performance on a laboratory memory test in healthy older adults, with a confidence interval excluding zero, while self-reported everyday function was unchanged. What does this establish?
lessons.answer: It establishes a blinded short-term effect on a laboratory performance measure in this sample; it does not establish benefit to everyday function, because that outcome did not change and a laboratory test score is a surrogate for the outcome that would matter.
lessons.distractor: It establishes that the compound improves memory, because double blinding removes expectancy and the confidence interval shows the laboratory effect is real.
lessons.correction: Blinding removes one class of bias, not all, and a real effect on a surrogate is not the same as benefit on the outcome that patients care about. The framework paper on surrogate endpoints makes exactly this distinction: an intermediate measure such as a test score can be interpretable as a stand-in only when there is evidence linking it to how people feel, function or survive, and here the direct functional measure was unchanged, which is evidence against the link rather than merely absent evidence for it. Additional questions decide how much the result can bear: was the effect size clinically meaningful, was the follow-up long enough for functional change to appear, was the sample representative, were adverse effects reported, and does the effect survive independent replication? The distractor treats blinding as a guarantee of validity and a confidence interval as a guarantee of importance; both are category errors.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms: randomisation assigns participants by chance; allocation concealment prevents recruiters from knowing or influencing the next assignment; blinding withholds condition from participants, staff, assessors or analysts; an active control is a comparison intervention intended to equalise expectancy and engagement; a sham or similar-form control mimics the structure of the intervention without its hypothesised ingredient; a surrogate endpoint is an intermediate outcome used in place of the clinical outcome of interest; a clinical outcome concerns how a person feels, functions or survives; statistical power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it exists; expectancy is a participant's belief about what the intervention will do; effect size standardisation expresses a difference in standard deviation units so that studies can be compared. Two cautions: statistical significance is a statement about compatibility with a null hypothesis, not about importance, and a blinded trial's estimate applies to the population and conditions sampled.
depth.mechanism: Why is the design feature - blinding or active control - what carries the inference? Because the causal claim requires excluding alternatives that produce the same observation. In a drug trial, the alternatives are expectancy, the act of taking something, and extra contact; an identical placebo removes them, leaving the pharmacological effect as the explanation of a between-arm difference, provided allocation was concealed and the outcome assessment was blinded too. In a behavioural trial, an equivalent sham cannot be constructed because the participant's own action is the intervention: practice, effort and belief all scale with the real intervention, so a similar-form control reduces but does not eliminate the advantage. The partial fixes are known and reported in the methodology review: measure expectations in both arms, match contact time, pre-specify the primary outcome, use objective rather than self-reported outcomes where possible, and report the pattern of results across measures rather than selecting the favourable ones. There is also a deeper limitation that no design fixes: both kinds of trial estimate effects on the measures they chose, and the leap from a test score to a life outcome requires a separate argument - the surrogate-endpoint problem - which the MCI meta-analysis illustrates with a small effect on global cognitive test performance and no automatic implication for how those participants functioned.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the two designs answering the same question: can a short intervention improve memory in healthy older adults? The behavioural version might randomise 200 volunteers to six weeks of practice on a memory strategy, an active control that spends the same time on a different mental activity, or a waiting list, with primary outcome a delayed-recall test and secondary outcomes self-reported memory and a functional questionnaire. Its strengths: low cost, easy follow-up, everyday measures feasible. Its threats: participants know which condition they are in, so any advantage may partly reflect effort and belief, and expectations must be measured and reported. The pharmacological version might randomise 200 volunteers to a compound or matching placebo with the same outcomes, with adverse events recorded. Its strengths: matching expectancy is straightforward and assessor blinding is possible. Its threats: on-treatment effects may not persist after the exposure stops, the sample excludes people with conditions that would complicate safety, and a test-score effect may not translate into function. Now the important point: the two designs do not supply independent evidence for one another. A positive behavioural result in the presence of unmeasured expectancy is not corroborated by a positive drug result, because the two studies have different confound structures and different mechanisms; convergence requires designs that exclude the same alternatives, or a replication of each with its own confounds addressed.
depth.mistake: Four errors are worth naming. The first is treating double blinding as a general guarantee of validity; it addresses expectancy and assessment bias only, and a blinded trial can still be underpowered, measure a surrogate, or generalise poorly. The second is treating statistical significance as importance: with a large enough sample, trivial differences become significant, and the confidence interval, not the p value, tells you what range of effects is compatible with the data. The third is assuming that a validated intervention must work in every format, or that a brain-based rationale validates an intervention; plausibility is not evidence, and mechanism language is used heavily in marketing for exactly that reason. The fourth is applying treatment guidance from a trial to an individual; this course teaches how to read trials, and the decision about any specific intervention for any specific person requires a clinician who knows the person. Diagnostic habit: whenever you read about an intervention, write down the comparison condition, the primary outcome, the power, and the follow-up length before you read the result.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take one published abstract of an intervention study - any design - and complete a five-line audit before reading the conclusion. Line 1: the comparison condition, named by type (inactive, active-ingredient, similar-form, no-contact). Line 2: the primary outcome, labelled surrogate or clinical. Line 3: the sample size and the standardised effect that size could detect at 80 per cent power. Line 4: expectations or blinding, and whether blinding integrity is reported. Line 5: follow-up length and what it permits you to claim. Model response: 'Comparison: similar-form control, expectancy not measured. Primary outcome: laboratory memory test - surrogate. n = 45 per group; detectable effect at 80 per cent power is about 0.6 SD, so smaller effects cannot be assessed. Blinding: participants unblinded, assessors blinded. Follow-up: eight weeks, so claims about long-term change are unsupported.' Self-review rubric: two points for correctly typing the comparison condition; two for labelling the outcome as surrogate or clinical with a reason; two for the power figure; two for a final statement restricted to the three things the design can support. A claim that the intervention works because the rationale is biological earns no points.
depth.summary: Drug and behavioural trials establish different things because the design feature that excludes alternatives differs: blinded matching for pharmacological effects, and matched engagement with measured expectations for behavioural ones. Expectancy alone can produce cognitive gains of the size that many training studies report, surrogate outcomes do not automatically stand for how people feel or function, and power arithmetic determines whether a null or a positive result carries information in the first place. Use the four-question audit - comparison condition, primary outcome type, power, follow-up - on every intervention claim, and keep the boundary clear between reading evidence and deciding about a person. Lesson 70 assembles all of this into an end-to-end evaluation of a commercial brain-training claim.
