lessons.title: Capstone: evaluating a commercial brain-training claim end to end
lessons.explanation: Objective: by the end of this lesson you should be able to take a marketing claim about brain training, restate it as a testable proposition, run a seven-step audit against the published evidence, and deliver a verdict with a stated confidence and a list of findings that would change it. This lesson is education about evaluating claims; it is not advice about any product, and it offers no guidance about anyone's health. Step one: restate the claim precisely. Marketing language is deliberately broad, so the first task is conversion. A verifiable version of a typical claim would be: regular practice on the product's games improves performance on everyday cognitive tasks in healthy adults and delays age-related cognitive decline. The public record gives a concrete case. In January 2016 the Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement with the makers of the Lumosity brain-training programme, under which the company would pay two million dollars in redress and notify subscribers of the action while providing an easy way to cancel auto-renewal. The press release states that the agency alleged the defendants deceived consumers with unfounded claims that the games can help users perform better at work and in school, and reduce or delay cognitive impairment associated with age and other serious health conditions, and it lists allegations that the claims covered improving everyday performance at work, in school and in athletics; delaying age-related cognitive decline and protecting against mild cognitive impairment, dementia and Alzheimer's disease; and reducing cognitive impairment associated with health conditions. Note the procedural status precisely: this is a settled enforcement action, and the agency's allegations are not a court's findings after trial. That distinction belongs in any honest account. Step two: classify each component. Improvement at work or school is a far-transfer and functional claim. Delaying decline is a longitudinal clinical claim about a population. Protection against named diseases is a disease-prevention claim. Step three: specify the design that could test each. A randomised trial with an active control, measured expectations, a pre-specified untrained primary outcome that measures function rather than a training-like task, and a follow-up of years for the decline claim. Step four: assemble what exists. One review of far transfer across chess, music and working memory training reports negative evidence, and a meta-analytic review by the same team states that the overall effect of far transfer is null and that the treatment-versus-active-control estimate is close to zero. The strongest long-term counterexample is the ACTIVE trial, which randomised older adults to memory, reasoning or speed-of-processing training or to a control condition, retained 44 per cent of participants at ten years, and reported effects on cognition and on performance-based measures of daily function that its own discussion characterises as tests of several abilities at once - which is a step towards function but still not a measure of whether people managed their lives differently. Step five: weigh the legal record as a signal, not as science; enforcement action indicates that a regulator judged the claims unsubstantiated, which is informative about the claims' backing, not about efficacy. Step six: cost. A subscription at about 15 dollars a month is about 180 dollars a year, or about 540 dollars over three years, which is the comparison price for whatever evidence the product can marshal. Step seven: verdict with language calibrated to the evidence and a list of what would change it. Three qualifications. First, the trained task does improve; near transfer is expected, and the question is only whether anything else does. Second, absence of evidence for far transfer is a finding about the literature, not a proof that no product could ever show it. Third, the ACTIVE results show that claims in this area are not all empty, which is precisely why the audit must be run per claim rather than per industry.
lessons.example: Run the numbers from the audit. First, convert an advertising phrase into a quantity. Suppose a product states that users become 20 per cent better at memory. Twenty per cent of what? If the baseline mean on a memory test is 50 points and the standard deviation is 15, a 20 per cent improvement is 10 raw points, or 0.67 standard deviations. If the baseline is 80 points on the same scale, 20 per cent is 16 points, or 1.07 standard deviations. The phrase is scale-dependent, so it must be converted before it can be compared with anything, and it cannot be compared with a published effect until both are on the same scale. Second, place the claim against the effect sizes and power requirements you have computed in this unit. Detecting 0.2 standard deviations with 80 per cent power takes about 393 participants per group; 0.1 takes about 1,570. The relevant meta-analytic estimate for far transfer against an active control is close to zero, and the MCI training meta-analysis found a standardised effect of 0.23 with a confidence interval from 0.03 to 0.44 on a cognitive test - small, wide, and measured on a surrogate. Third, the expectancy arithmetic from the placebo study: a recruitment framing alone was associated with about 0.5 standard deviations of fluid-intelligence change, roughly 6 to 8 IQ points on that scale, which is larger than most reported training effects. So a product's unpublished or weak-controlled study with 40 participants per group and an unblinded self-selected sample is not merely uninformative; the artefacts available to it are bigger than the effect it wants to claim. Fourth, cost. At 14.99 dollars per month, one year costs 14.99 x 12 = 179.88 dollars, and three years cost 14.99 x 36 = 539.64 dollars. Present the arithmetic as a comparison the reader can hold: about 540 dollars over three years against a far-transfer estimate near zero on the evidence, with a strong long-term trial in the same field showing modest test-based gains and incomplete retention. That juxtaposition, not the adjective 'unproven', is what a defensible verdict looks like.
lessons.question: A reviewer of your capstone audit objects that the ACTIVE trial supports the marketing claim, because trained participants showed effects on measures of daily function ten years later. How should the audit respond?
lessons.answer: The ACTIVE result supports a narrow and real claim, that a specific training programme produced lasting gains on the measures used, but the criteria for the marketing claim are untrained functional outcomes and a demonstration of delayed clinical decline, and the trial's own discussion describes the daily-function measures as tests that draw on several cognitive abilities rather than as direct measures of how people manage their lives.
lessons.distractor: The ACTIVE result should be discarded because its ten-year retention was only 44 per cent, which makes the trial uninformative about long-term effects.
lessons.correction: Discarding the trial for attrition is too strong: attrition reduces precision and raises questions about who remained, but 44 per cent retention over ten years in an older adult sample is a substantial follow-up, and the paper reports the comparison against the control condition rather than only within-group change. The correct move is calibration, not dismissal. The marketing claim has three components - improvement in everyday performance, delayed decline, and protection against named diseases - and ACTIVE addresses a version of the first and, at most, early markers related to the second. Its outcome measures are performance-based tests of several abilities, which is why the authors themselves qualify them, and it does not test protection against dementia. A good audit therefore cites ACTIVE as the strongest positive evidence in the field and then specifies exactly how far it reaches, which strengthens the audit's credibility rather than weakening it. Compare the negative far-transfer reviews, which estimate the general case against active controls, and present both: the verdict rests on the pattern, not on one study.

depth.definitions: Prerequisite terms carried from earlier lessons: far transfer is improvement on tasks dissimilar to the trained one; an active control equalises expectancy and engagement; expectancy is the participant's belief about what an intervention will do; a surrogate endpoint is an intermediate measure used in place of the outcome that matters; near transfer is improvement on the trained or closely similar task, which is expected. Add three terms specific to evaluating commercial claims. Substantiation means the evidence a seller holds for a claim; in advertising regulation this is the standard a claim must meet, and it is not identical to the scientific standard, so an enforcement outcome tells you about the claim's backing rather than about the underlying science. A settled enforcement action means the parties reached an agreement; the allegations are the regulator's, and the settlement is not an admission of liability unless stated as such. Calibration means choosing language whose strength matches the evidence, so that a verdict says what a pattern of studies supports and what it does not test.
depth.mechanism: Why would a product built on real laboratory findings still fail to deliver the advertised generalisations? Four mechanisms explain the gap, and each is measurable. The first is specificity: practice improves the representations engaged by the practised task, so improvement is largest where the task overlaps. The second is expectation: unblinded training with an appealing narrative produces gains on the outcome measure through expectancy and effort, which the placebo study demonstrated with identical training and different recruitment framing. The third is measurement choice: studies that report the training-like task as the outcome will show gains, while the claims concern other tasks and function. The fourth is selection and attrition: participants who sign up and stay are a selected group, and the effects in that group need not extend to those the marketing addresses. Note what would distinguish a successful product from these mechanisms: an untrained, functionally meaningful primary outcome; an active control with measured expectations; adequate power for the effect being claimed; a follow-up long enough for the decline claim; and replication by researchers without a stake in the product. That list is the audit's spine, and every product-level verdict should be traceable to which items are satisfied.
depth.secondExample: Run the same seven-step audit on a claim from a different domain, physical exercise and cognition, to show that the procedure is not a machine for producing scepticism. Step one: restate. Regular aerobic exercise improves several aspects of health and is associated with better cognitive outcomes in older adults. Step two: classify. Health outcomes are clinical; cognitive outcomes include test-based measures. Step three: design. Randomised trials with functional and clinical outcomes, long follow-up, and attention-matched controls. Step four: evidence. Physical activity has well-established effects on cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes, and cognitive benefits are supported with more variable estimates than those cardiovascular effects, with heterogeneity across populations and measures. Step five: regulatory record. Exercise is not advertised with disease-prevention claims in the way supplements and training applications are, so the record is thinner and less informative. Step six: cost. The comparison is not a subscription but a change in routine, whose costs and risks differ in kind. Step seven: verdict. The claim survives in a calibrated form for health outcomes and in a weaker form for cognition, with the strength of evidence concentrated where the measurement is clinical. The contrast is instructive: the audit does not reject claims; it reports where the evidence is strong, where it is thin, and where the claim as written exceeds both. That is the difference between calibrated appraisal and reflexive dismissal.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur in evaluating these products. The first is treating an enforcement action as proof of inefficacy, or its absence as proof of efficacy: the FTC case concerns substantiation of advertising claims and was settled, so it informs you about the claims' backing, not about whether training does something. The second is dismissing the whole enterprise because far transfer is unsupported, which ignores that the trained task genuinely improves and that the ACTIVE trial produced durable test-based gains. The third is accepting a peer-reviewed study as sufficient when it lacks an active control, measured expectations and adequate power, since those are the design features that determine what even a carefully run study can show. The fourth is answering a different question from the one asked: a study of children, of a clinical population, or of a laboratory task cannot support a claim aimed at healthy adults' everyday function. The diagnostic habit for this lesson is to keep a written list of the seven steps and to mark each one as satisfied, unsatisfied, or not tested, which converts an argument into an audit.
depth.application: Capstone task, nonblocking. Produce a 400-word evaluation of one real brain-training or cognitive-enhancement advertisement, following the seven steps: restate the claim as testable propositions; classify each component as near transfer, far transfer, functional or disease-prevention; state the design that could test it; report the evidence you can find, naming at least two studies including one that supports at least part of the claim; state the regulatory or legal record if any, with its procedural status; compute the annual and three-year cost of the product; and deliver a calibrated verdict with three findings that would change it. Model response structure: 'Claim restated: six weeks of daily game play improves untrained working-memory tasks in healthy adults (far transfer, test-based). Design required: randomised, active control, expectations measured, pre-specified untrained primary outcome, n sized for a small effect. Evidence: meta-analytic estimate for far transfer against active control near zero; long-term training trial showing durable gains on multi-ability test composites. Regulatory record: settled enforcement action in 2016 concerning advertising substantiation; allegations, not court findings. Cost: 179.88 dollars per year, 539.64 over three years. Verdict: the trained-game improvement is credible and near transfer is expected; the far-transfer and everyday-function claims are not supported by the evidence I found. Would change my verdict: a preregistered randomised trial with an active control, measured expectations, adequate power, and an untrained functional primary outcome showing benefit, replicated by an independent group, plus functional outcomes that persist after training ends.' Self-review rubric: two points for a testable restatement; two for naming the required design features; three for using at least two real sources with their limits stated; two for the cost arithmetic; two for a verdict whose language matches the evidence and a genuinely specific change-my-mind list.
depth.summary: A commercial cognitive-training claim is appraised like any other multi-part claim: convert it to testable propositions, classify them, specify the design that could test each, assemble the evidence including the strongest supportive study, weigh the regulatory record with its procedural status, do the cost arithmetic, and deliver a calibrated verdict with conditions that would change it. The consistent findings across this level are that the trained task improves, expectation and poor controls inflate apparent benefits, untrained far-transfer effects are near zero against active controls, and the strongest long-term trial shows modest gains on multi-ability test measures with substantial attrition. The intellectual content of this capstone is not a verdict about one product; it is the reusable procedure, the arithmetic that keeps claims on a common scale, and the habit of stating what would change your mind. That procedure transfers to any claim you will meet about the brain, which is the point of the course.

questions.prompt: A laboratory reports that administering a drug after a reminder cue reduced a conditioned fear response at 24 hours, and concludes that the memory was erased. A colleague argues that the same reduction would appear if the memory were intact but harder to retrieve. Which single addition to the design would most directly address the colleague's alternative?
questions.answer: A later test using a different reminder cue or a different response measure, to determine whether the memory can still be expressed when it is accessed by another route.
questions.distractor: A larger sample, because the disagreement is essentially about whether the observed reduction is statistically reliable enough to support the erasure claim.
questions.correction: Increasing the sample addresses precision, not the interpretation of the effect, and the effect itself is what the two accounts both predict, which is why the dispute is about what it means rather than whether it happened. The retrieval-failure account predicts that the memory remains available to another cue or can be observed through another measure, whereas an erasure account predicts that no route recovers it. The relevant addition is therefore a test of recovery or an independent expression measure - both predictions are stated in advance, and the result discriminates between them. This is the same rival-explanation discipline used in lesson 66, where the review's box on alternative interpretations of retrieval-dependent amnesia collects exactly such alternatives, and it is why a single reduction in one readout cannot settle the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A study finds that participants who report frequent media multitasking score lower on a measure of distractor filtering, with r = 0.15 in a sample of 60 undergraduates. A commentary calls this a strong demonstration that heavy media use damages attentional control. Which two criticisms from this unit apply most directly?
questions.answer: The estimated association is small and estimated imprecisely - r = 0.15 explains about 2 per cent of the variance and a sample of 60 is far too small to estimate an effect this size - and the design cannot establish direction, since the questionnaire measures a self-reported habit and the outcome is measured concurrently.
questions.distractor: The measure of distractor filtering is invalid because laboratory tasks cannot index real-world attention, and the participants were undergraduates rather than a representative sample.
questions.correction: The distractor's criticisms are generic and, in the second case, a generalisability caveat rather than the reason to reject the inference. The two criticisms that follow from this unit are quantitative and structural. Quantitatively, r = 0.15 corresponds to about 2 per cent of variance, and detecting a correlation of 0.15 at conventional power requires a sample in the hundreds, so a sample of 60 cannot furnish the precision the word strong implies; this is the arithmetic behind the meta-analytic finding that the association is weak and loses significance once small-study effects are corrected. Structurally, the predictor is a self-report about behaviour and the outcome is measured at the same time, so a preference explanation and a damage explanation are equally compatible with the data. Compare lesson 67 and the two replication studies and meta-analysis of 39 effect sizes.

questions.prompt: A coach recommends that a player build a new warm-up routine by an if-then plan, and predicts that the routine will become insensitive to whether it actually helps performance. A colleague objects that the routine is clearly changing because the player drops it whenever the team switches to a different schedule. Who is right, and why?
questions.answer: The colleague has the better argument: dropping the routine when the schedule changes shows the behaviour still tracks its outcomes and context rather than being cue-triggered in an outcome-insensitive way, so the evidence points to goal-directed control with a well-learned habit of doing it.
questions.distractor: The coach is right, because any behaviour performed consistently in the same context becomes habitual, and evidence of dropping it is simply a sign that the habit had not formed yet.
questions.correction: The distractor treats repetition and context stability as sufficient for habitual control, which is the misconception this lesson targets. Habitual control is defined operationally by insensitivity to outcome value and to the action-outcome contingency, and the coach's prediction was an insensitivity prediction. The observation is that the player drops the routine when circumstances change, which is the signature of outcome sensitivity, so the prediction failed and goal-directed control remains the better description. Note the second point the coach's own evidence supports: cue-based plans are studied precisely because they move the initiation of a behaviour to a stable situation, reducing the need for daily deliberation, which is compatible with the routine remaining goal-sensitive. See lesson 68 and the review's section questioning the assumption that habits are uniquely sticky.

questions.prompt: Two trials test the same memory-training programme in healthy older adults. Trial A gives the programme versus a waiting list, finds a significant improvement on the trained task, and reports that participants reported higher confidence that memory can be improved. Trial B gives the programme versus a similar-form activity matched for time, measures expectations in both arms, and finds no difference on the trained task. What is the most defensible comparison of the two?
questions.answer: Trial B is the more informative test because it matches contact and expectancy and checks whether that matching succeeded, while Trial A leaves both uncontrolled and reports a confidence difference that is consistent with the expectancy explanation.
questions.distractor: Trial A is more informative because it found a significant result, whereas Trial B may simply have been underpowered to detect the same improvement.
questions.correction: Significance is not informativeness. Trial A's design contains exactly the features that produce apparent effects without training: a waiting-list comparison leaves expectancy, contact time and the reward of taking part uncontrolled, and the reported group difference in belief about memory improvement is evidence that expectations differed between arms. Trial B's null result is compatible with a genuine absence of an effect on that measure, and its active-control structure means an absence is meaningful rather than merely underpowered-and-unknown, provided the study reports its detectable effect size. The objection about power is legitimate only if Trial B's precision was poor, in which case the correct conclusion is that the trial was uninformative rather than that Trial A was better - which is the reason to require a stated power calculation, as in lesson 69 and the placebo-control review.

questions.prompt: An advertisement says that the product is supported by a study showing improvements on the tasks it trains, by a ten-year randomised trial in older adults showing lasting effects on measures of daily function, and by the absence of any regulatory action against the company. You must produce a calibrated verdict. Which statement is best?
questions.answer: The trained-task improvement is credible and expected as near transfer; the ten-year trial is genuine but its functional measures are tests drawing on several abilities and its claim does not reach disease prevention or everyday performance; and the absence of regulatory action is not evidence of efficacy.
questions.distractor: The three elements converge, so the advertisement's claim is supported: a randomised trial provides the causal evidence, and the study on trained tasks shows the mechanism by which the benefit arises.
questions.correction: The three elements do not converge on the advertised claim because each speaks to a different proposition with a different evidential standard. Near transfer to the trained task is expected and is not evidence of generalisation. The randomised trial supplies the strongest evidence in the field for durable gains on cognitive and multi-ability measures, and its own discussion qualifies what those measures are, so it supports a narrower claim than the advertisement makes; disease prevention and everyday performance remain untested by it. And an absence of enforcement action says nothing about efficacy, since advertising regulation concerns substantiation of the claims a seller makes, and enforcement is discretionary and retrospective. The calibrated verdict therefore reports the pattern, states which components are supported, and names the findings that would change the assessment - which is the seven-step procedure in lesson 70.

questions.prompt: A laboratory reports that a brief visuomotor rotation training session changed the direction-tuning curves of a small set of motor cortex neurons, and a commentary concludes that the rotation task's internal model is encoded in those neurons. A second laboratory reports that after the same rotation training, a transcranial magnetic stimulation protocol that transiently disrupts the same region abolishes the after-effect for about twenty minutes and then the after-effect returns. Explain what each result supports, why the second is not a refutation of the first, and what further evidence the encoding claim requires.
questions.answer: The first result shows that direction tuning changes with training, which establishes involvement and representation; the second shows that the region is necessary for expressing the after-effect during the disruption window, which is a necessity result that is compatible with the change being stored there, distributed elsewhere, or read out through that region; an encoding claim needs evidence that the measured change is specific to the trained condition, tracks the size of the behavioural after-effect across participants, and persists over the retention interval that the behaviour persists.
questions.distractor: The second result shows that the region cannot be the storage site, because if the memory were stored there, disrupting the region would abolish it permanently rather than for twenty minutes.
questions.correction: Temporary disruption and storage are different questions, and the distractor conflates the two. A disruption that temporarily removes a behavioural expression tells you the disrupted tissue is necessary for performance during the window, not that it is the enduring substrate; the after-effect's return shows that something survived the disruption, which could be a store elsewhere or a store in that region that resumes function when the disruption ends, since the intervention is transient by construction. The first result has the opposite limitation: a change in tuning curves is a representation result and cannot, on its own, distinguish a change that stores the skill from a change that accompanies it, nor does it rule out the possibility that the relevant variable is represented elsewhere and merely relayed through the recorded region. This is the necessity-sufficiency-selective-inference logic you met earlier in the course, and it applies to skill claims exactly as it does to other causal claims about the brain. Circumscribing evidence, not a single dramatic result, is what converts a representation finding into a storage claim.

questions.prompt: A cognitive-training company cites three studies: a randomised trial showing improved performance on the trained task; a cross-sectional study showing that long-term users of the product have different brain activity from non-users; and a study showing that a subgroup of high responders improved on an untrained memory test after a further analysis. You must explain, for each, what it can support and what single design change would make it more probative, and then state the overall evidential position carefully.
questions.answer: The randomised trial supports near transfer to the trained task and would become probative for a broader claim only if the primary outcome were an untrained functional measure with an active control; the cross-sectional brain-activity difference is consistent with selection and with training and would become informative with a longitudinal design in the same people; the subgroup result is exploratory after-the-fact and would become informative if the subgroup and outcome were pre-specified and independently replicated.
questions.distractor: The three studies together are stronger than any one alone, because randomised evidence for the mechanism combines with observational evidence for real-world users and with a significant effect in the responsive subgroup to support the general claim.
questions.correction: Three weak studies do not add up to one strong study when each is weak in a different way, because the weaknesses concern the same inferential gap rather than independent parts of it. The randomised trial's outcome is the trained task, so it addresses a proposition the company does not need to prove. The brain-activity comparison has the structure of an expertise comparison, so it cannot separate the product from the kind of person who persists with it. The subgroup analysis has no pre-specification and is exactly the kind of analysis in which a false positive is expected: with several subgroup tests at conventional thresholds, a significant result somewhere is unsurprising. The combined position is therefore a set of results that are each individually compatible with the product doing what it claims and with it doing nothing beyond what practice and expectation deliver, and the design changes listed are what would begin to discriminate. Compute the arithmetic too: if the untrained-test effect is small, the study needs hundreds of participants to estimate it, so a subgroup of high responders is very unlikely to be adequate.

questions.prompt: A school considers a policy based on the claim that learning a second language must begin before age seven. Supporting evidence is offered in three pieces: a study in which late learners score lower on average on a grammaticality test that has a maximum score reached by many early learners; a reanalysis showing a significant quadratic term for age of onset in a regression; and an animal study on monocular deprivation. For each piece, state what it supports, and give the overall verdict on the policy premise.
questions.answer: The first shows an average group difference on a bounded measure, which compresses high performers and cannot support a categorical deadline; the quadratic term shows that a nonlinear model fits better in that sample, which is a statement about the fit of one specification and is sensitive to how age is entered and whether age at testing is partialled out; the animal study supports a mechanism for timed deprivation effects in another species. The premise of a hard deadline before seven is not supported; a graded sensitive period with wide individual variation is supported.
questions.distractor: The three pieces are mutually corroborating, so the premise is supported: the bounded test shows the effect in people, the quadratic term identifies the breakpoint at about age seven, and the animal study supplies the mechanism that explains why the breakpoint exists.
questions.correction: Corroboration requires the pieces to exclude the same alternatives, and these do not. A bounded test leaves little room at the top, so the late-learning group is squeezed into a narrow band and the estimated breakpoint moves; the quadratic term is a fitted parameter whose location depends on the specification and on confounds such as age at testing, which is why the statistical critique in this level treats it as a modelling decision to be justified rather than a discovered boundary; and cross-species mechanism evidence constrains what is biologically possible without fixing a human age. Note also what none of the three measures: the quality and quantity of the learners' exposure, their instruction, and how proficiency was assessed, which are the confounds a natural experiment cannot remove. The defensible policy premise, if one is needed, is that earlier exposure on average yields better outcomes on demanding measures with wide overlap, which supports offering early opportunities without asserting that later learners cannot succeed. That is the difference between an average gradient and a deadline.

questions.prompt: A research team tests the dual-systems account of adolescent risk taking with three analyses on one dataset of 60 adolescents: a cross-sectional correlation between a reward-reactivity index and risk taking, a comparison of mean reward reactivity between two age groups, and a median split on an imbalance score with a t-test between the resulting subgroups. Evaluate each analysis and state what a within-person test would require.
questions.answer: The cross-sectional correlation cannot support temporal precedence and is likely attenuated by an unreliable difference or reactivity measure; the age-group mean comparison confounds age with cohort and with everything that differs between the groups and cannot show within-person change; the median split discards information and creates a comparison whose groups are defined by the outcome variable's own distribution, which inflates apparent contrast and reduces reliability. A within-person test needs repeated measurement of both constructs in the same people on at least three occasions, a pre-specified imbalance specification with reported reliability, and a time-ordered prediction.
questions.distractor: The three analyses are convergent because they all point in the same direction, and the median-split comparison is the strongest of the three because it directly contrasts participants with high and low imbalance.
questions.correction: Convergence across analyses that share the same dataset and the same confounds is not independent corroboration, and the median split is the weakest of the three, not the strongest. Splitting a continuous, unreliably measured score at the median creates two groups whose difference is partly noise, throws away the information in the middle, and if the split is chosen after inspecting the data, becomes an undisclosed multiple comparison. The age-group comparison faces the cohort problem that plagues every cross-sectional developmental design, and its group means cannot show that any individual's imbalance preceded their own risk taking, which is what the model's causal structure requires. The within-person version is demanding by design: it asks whether a person's larger-than-usual imbalance predicts their own subsequent risk taking, which needs several occasions and a reliable change measure. If the construct cannot be measured reliably enough to support that test, the correct conclusion is that the theory is currently under-tested rather than that the theory is wrong.

questions.prompt: A memory clinic advertises a screening package using three tests, each with reported sensitivity around 85 per cent and specificity around 85 per cent, and states that a positive result on any one test indicates early impairment. A patient scores below the cut-off on one test. Using the reasoning of this level, explain how the any-one-test rule changes the properties of the package, what would be required to interpret the result for this person, and why a single score cannot bear the claim.
questions.answer: Combining tests with an any-positive rule raises sensitivity but lowers specificity, so in a low-prevalence population the number of false positives grows and a positive result on one test carries a low probability of true impairment; interpreting a result for this person requires a change from their own earlier level on a measure with known reliability, information about function, and an accounting for education, language, hearing, mood and medication effects.
questions.distractor: Using three tests rather than one makes a positive result more trustworthy, because three independent measurements agreeing that something is abnormal is stronger evidence than a single measurement.
questions.correction: The any-positive rule is not an agreement rule: it produces a positive result when a single test is abnormal, so it maximises the chance of catching true cases and maximises false positives at the same time. Work the arithmetic with a 5 per cent prevalence: at 85 per cent specificity a single test produces 142 false positives per 1,000 people and about 43 true positives, so a single positive result is more likely to be a false positive than a true one, and requiring only one abnormal test keeps that ratio. The proposed alternative - requiring all three to be abnormal - would flip the trade-off, raising specificity and missing more cases. Either rule is a policy choice about which errors you prefer, and the advertisement presents it as though it were a property of the tests. For an individual, a below-cut-off score on one occasion is one noisy measurement; the informative comparison is with the person's own prior level, using the reliable-change threshold for that test, alongside functional information. Any interpretation for a real person belongs with a qualified clinician; the lesson's contribution is the arithmetic and the question structure.

questions.prompt: You are asked to review a manuscript claiming that a drug given after retrieval erases a fear memory in humans. The manuscript reports a reduction in startle potentiation at 24 hours, no manipulation check on the drug's physiological effect, no measure of whether the reminder produced prediction error, an administered-versus-placebo comparison with randomisation but no blinding of participants, and a secondary analysis showing the effect in participants who reported being surprised by the reminder. Explain which of these features undermine the erasure claim and how, and what the surprise subgroup analysis does and does not add.
questions.answer: Without a manipulation check the negative result could be a failed administration rather than a failed mechanism; without a prediction-error measure the design cannot establish the precondition the hypothesis requires, so a negative outcome is uninformative about the mechanism and a positive outcome is unconstrained; without participant blinding, expectancy can produce the reduction; and the surprise subgroup is an exploratory analysis of a measure that should have been collected for everyone and used prospectively, so its addition is at best hypothesis-generating and at worst a selected comparison.
questions.distractor: The design is adequate because it randomised and used a placebo comparison; the remaining features are refinements that affect the precision of the estimate rather than the validity of the erasure conclusion.
questions.correction: Randomisation and a placebo control address selection and the passage of time, but they do not address expectancy when participants know which treatment they received, and they do not license a mechanism claim. Three separate requirements are missing here. The manipulation check establishes that the intervention did what it was supposed to physiologically, without which a null or small effect cannot be interpreted. The prediction-error measure establishes that the precondition the hypothesis names was actually met; without it, the study cannot distinguish a failed hypothesis from a failed induction, which is why the review in this level treats prediction error as a requirement rather than a detail. Blinding removes the expectancy route to reduced responding, which the placebo study in this level showed can be large. The surprise subgroup is the weakest element: the moderator was measured after the fact, the comparison was not pre-specified, and the sample within the subgroup is smaller still, so it cannot carry the claim. A well-designed version would pre-register all three elements and report them for the whole sample.

questions.prompt: A workplace introduces a policy of banning concurrent task performance, justified by three claims: that switching between tasks costs a fixed percentage of productive time, that high perceptual load eliminates distractibility, and that multitasking habits reduce attentional control. For each claim, state the evidence standard it would need and evaluate what the literature in this level actually provides.
questions.answer: The switching-cost claim needs a measured cost in a defined task with time-on-task held constant, and the fixed-percentage version usually cannot be traced to a study matching the situation; the load claim needs an independent definition of load and a pre-specified interference outcome, because otherwise the construct is defined by the outcome it is meant to explain; and the habit claim rests largely on self-report questionnaires, with the meta-analytic association weak and rendered nonsignificant after correction for small-study effects.
questions.distractor: All three claims are supported in principle, so the policy is justified: switching costs are established in laboratory experiments, load theory is a well-known account of distractor suppression, and the media-multitasking literature shows attentional differences between heavy and light users.
questions.correction: The distractor substitutes the existence of a phenomenon for the transfer of a specific quantity and ignores the internal disputes. Task-switching costs do exist and are measurable, but the popular practice of attaching a single percentage to all interruptions requires a study with those tasks, that interruption structure and that population; the number does not travel on its own. Load theory does predict reduced distractor processing under high load, but the critique in this level documents circularity when load is identified by the absence of interference and dilution as a rival explanation, so a citation to the theory is not enough - you need the design details. The media-multitasking association is small, measured by questionnaire, direction-ambiguous, and nonsignificant once small-study effects are corrected. A defensible policy statement would therefore cite the measured cost in a comparable task, justify the load manipulation if it is cited at all, and describe the multitasking evidence as weak and correlational. The policy might still be wise; the point is that the justification must match the evidence rather than borrowing the authority of a whole literature.

questions.prompt: A behaviour-change programme claims that a new routine will 'rewire' a habit within three weeks and that the routine will then persist regardless of whether it still helps. Evaluate both parts of the claim using the tests and evidence in this level, and describe the design that would test the persistence part.
questions.answer: The three-week timing asserts a fixed schedule that the habit-formation literature does not support, since time to maximal self-reported automaticity varies widely with behaviour complexity, cue stability and frequency; the persistence part asserts outcome insensitivity, which is the defining feature of habitual control and is testable with an outcome devaluation or contingency degradation procedure, ideally in the same people over time with a no-longer-beneficial outcome.
questions.distractor: Both parts are reasonable: repetition produces automaticity on a characteristic timescale, and automatic behaviour is by definition independent of its consequences, which is why it persists.
questions.correction: The distractor states two popular assumptions that the evidence in this level does not support. Automaticity in the laboratory sense means initiation with little deliberation, not immunity to consequences, and the review on habit and persistence examines resistance to extinction, contingency degradation, relapse and context change and argues that habit should not be equated with unusual stickiness. So the claim's second half is an empirical prediction that could turn out false, and it should be tested rather than asserted. The design that tests it needs three elements. First, an operational measure of habitual control, such as a devaluation or contingency degradation procedure, rather than a self-report of automaticity. Second, a time course, with the procedure administered repeatedly so that the transition, if it happens, is observed within people rather than inferred from a cross-sectional comparison. Third, a control condition in which the outcome remains valuable, so that any decline in responding can be attributed to the change in outcome value rather than to time or fatigue. Notice that the timing claim and the persistence claim are separate: even if automaticity develops quickly for a simple behaviour in a stable context, that says nothing about whether the behaviour will persist when its outcome changes.

questions.prompt: A trial reports that a twelve-week programme improved a laboratory measure of attention in older adults by 0.3 standard deviations compared with a no-contact control, that expectations were higher in the programme arm, and that no differences were found on self-reported everyday function. A commentary calls the result a proven cognitive benefit. Explain what each element of the trial does to the claim, compute what the numbers imply about scale and power, and state the verdict.
questions.answer: The 0.3 standard deviation change is a small effect on a laboratory surrogate; the no-contact comparison leaves expectancy and contact unmatched, and the measured expectation difference is evidence that this route was live; the null on everyday function is a failure to show benefit where it would matter. The verdict is a small, expectancy-confounded effect on a surrogate measure, not a proven cognitive benefit.
questions.distractor: The result is a proven cognitive benefit because the comparison was randomised and the effect, though small, was statistically detected against a control group.
questions.correction: Randomisation removes selection but not expectancy, and a no-contact control is precisely the design in which the placebo literature expects inflated effects; the trial even provides the relevant evidence by showing higher expectations in the programme arm, which is the pattern the placebo study in this level produced with an identical training procedure and different recruitment framing. On scale: 0.3 standard deviations on a laboratory attention task is smaller than the expectancy-associated change of about 0.5 standard deviations reported in that study, so the artefact available to the design is larger than the effect the trial claims to have isolated - a state of affairs that cannot be repaired by significance testing. On power: a study that detects an effect of 0.3 will typically have been sized for something near that value; if the true effect is smaller once expectancy is controlled, the design is underpowered for the honest estimate, and detecting 0.2 requires roughly 393 participants per group. The verdict, stated at the strength the evidence can bear: attention improved on the laboratory measure in a design where expectations differed between arms, and there is no evidence of improvement in everyday function. This is exactly the audit sequence from the final lesson of the level.

questions.prompt: A product's evidence package contains four items: a randomised trial of the product versus an active control published by the company's own researchers, showing no far transfer and a significant near-transfer effect; a mechanism paper showing that training changes activity in a task-relevant region; a peer-reviewed study showing a correlation between hours of use and self-rated sharpness; and a ten-year randomised trial of a different training format showing durable gains on multi-ability test composites. Write the calibrated verdict, stating for each item what it supports and naming the two findings that would most change the verdict.
questions.answer: The company trial supports the near-transfer effect and is itself evidence against the far-transfer claim, which is why its source does not disqualify it; the mechanism paper supports a change in task-related activity without establishing benefit or transfer; the hours-and-sharpness correlation is confounded by selection and self-report; and the ten-year trial supports durable gains on test-based measures of several abilities in a different programme, which is the strongest supportive element but not a functional or disease-prevention result. Findings that would change the verdict: a preregistered randomised trial with an active control, measured expectations, adequate power and an untrained functional primary outcome showing benefit; and replication of such a result by an independent group with functional gains persisting after training stops.
questions.distractor: The verdict should be that the product is supported: the company's own trial found a significant effect, the mechanism paper explains why it works, the correlation with reported sharpness shows real-world benefit, and the ten-year trial corroborates the general approach.
questions.correction: Each clause of the distractor overstates its item in the same direction, which is the diagnostic signature of a package rather than a set of independent proofs. Source and significance do not determine what a design shows: an adequately controlled trial that finds no far transfer is evidence against the far-transfer claim even when the sponsor ran it, and the significant near-transfer effect is exactly what practice on the trained task predicts. A mechanism result about task-related activity is a level-of-description finding and cannot show benefit or generalisation, which is the discipline from the earlier part of this level. The hours-and-sharpness correlation is confounded three ways - selection, self-report on both sides, and no control for expectations - so it is best described as a claim about what users report. The ten-year trial is the strongest item and deserves its due: randomised, long, with durable gains on test measures, and with the authors' own qualification that those functional measures draw on several abilities. A verdict that says so, and that names the two findings capable of changing it, is calibrated and falsifiable, which is the standard this capstone asks you to meet.

questions.prompt: A study in healthy older adults reports that six weeks of cognitive training improved a composite memory score by 0.25 standard deviations relative to an active control, and that a structural imaging measure of hippocampal volume increased slightly in the training arm. A commentary concludes that training protects the brain against ageing. Explain what the two results can and cannot support, how a surrogate-endpoint argument bears on the claim, and what would be needed for the protection claim.
questions.answer: The memory composite effect is a small improvement on a test measure relative to an active control, which supports a modest benefit on that measure; the volume change is a small structural difference that may accompany training, effort or measurement variation and does not establish protection; protection against ageing is a claim about clinical change over years, so it needs long follow-up with functional and clinical outcomes, and the test and volume measures are surrogates that require an argument linking them to those outcomes.
questions.distractor: The two results reinforce each other: a behavioural improvement alongside a structural change is convergent evidence that training altered the brain in a protective direction, because structure and function cannot both change by chance.
questions.correction: Convergence requires that the two results be independent measures of the same process, and here they are not obviously so. Both come from the same participants in the same trial, so any expectancy, effort or participation difference between arms affects both, which is exactly the pattern an active control is meant to limit but cannot eliminate when the participants know their condition. Structural measures also have their own variability, and a small change in a volume estimate over six weeks can reflect image acquisition and segmentation variation as easily as tissue change, which is why the measure needs a stated reliability and a pre-specified analysis. The surrogate-endpoint point cuts deepest: a memory composite and a volume estimate are both intermediate quantities, and the claim concerns how people function over years, so even a genuine improvement in both leaves the link to the clinical outcome to be established rather than assumed. A protection claim would need a randomised design with active control, measured expectations, pre-specified clinical and functional endpoints, follow-up of several years, and a stated effect size with its confidence interval, replicated independently. Anything less can support a narrower statement about the measures actually used.

questions.prompt: You must design one study that could, in principle, distinguish three explanations for why adolescent musicians perform better than non-musicians on an attention task: training-induced change, self-selection of people with better attention into music, and expectancy or motivation during testing. State the design, the measurement plan, and how each of the three explanations would be separated.
questions.answer: Randomise a defined population with no prior music training to a structured music programme or an active control matched for contact, time and enjoyment, measure attention on an untrained task with blinded assessors, collect a baseline prior to allocation and expectations after allocation in both arms, and follow participants over a period long enough for the training dose to accumulate; training would be supported by a between-arm difference on the pre-specified untrained outcome, selection by pre-existing baseline differences that predict who continues, and expectancy by measured expectations correlating with outcome within arms rather than between them.
questions.distractor: Compare musicians with non-musicians, control statistically for age, intelligence and socioeconomic status, and measure attention with a battery of tests; if the difference survives the covariates, the training explanation stands.
questions.correction: Covariate adjustment cannot do this work, because the confound is not an incomplete list of measured variables but the entire process by which people become and remain musicians, which includes attention, persistence, family resources, teacher effects and opportunity. Adjusting for covariates can even increase bias when the covariates are consequences of the selection process, and it cannot address expectancy during testing at all. The randomised design addresses selection directly, since allocation is by chance and baseline measures should then be balanced - which is also why the baseline is the diagnostic for selection, because an imbalance at baseline would reveal that the randomisation did not deliver comparable groups. The active control with measured expectations addresses the third explanation, and the requirement that the outcome be untrained and assessed by blinded assessors prevents the near-transfer route from masquerading as an attention benefit. Two honest limitations belong in the design statement: a study long enough to accumulate a meaningful dose of musical training is expensive and will have attrition, and the attention measure must be pre-specified with adequate power, since the plausible effects are small and the arithmetic for detecting them demands hundreds of participants per arm. Stating those limits, rather than hiding them, is what makes the design credible.
